title: A Symmetry-Aware Exploration of Bayesian Neural Network Posteriors
submission: The distribution of modern deep neural networks (DNNs) weights -- crucial for uncertainty quantification and robustness -- is an eminently complex object due to its extremely high dimensionality. This paper presents an exploration of the posterior distribution of deep Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs), extending its study to common vision tasks and architectures. We broadly discuss approaches for approximating the posterior, and touch on relationships between posterior quality and uncertainty estimation, without committing to a single best practice. We also consider how modes in the posterior and simple visualization techniques relate to these issues. Moreover, we highlight weight-space symmetries as an important factor for interpreting the posterior, and provide a qualitative assessment of permutation and scaling symmetries and their interaction with L2 regularization. To support further work, we release a large-scale checkpoint dataset of real-world models together with code, intended to enable additional explorations rather than definitive conclusions.

title: Prompt Curriculum Learning for Efficient LLM Post-Training
submission: Reinforcement learning is widely used to post-train large language models for tasks such as mathematical reasoning and coding. Convergence of RL training depends on batching and prompt selection strategies. We investigate factors that affect convergence including batch size and prompt difficulty across models and datasets. We find there is an interplay between generation time and gradient quality, and that prompts of intermediate difficulty tend to be informative for training. Motivated by these observations, we propose Prompt Curriculum Learning (PCL), an algorithm that selects intermediate-difficulty prompts using a learned value model to avoid costly rollouts and guide training toward informative samples. Empirically, PCL is compared to rollout-based filtering across several benchmarks and shows practical differences in training efficiency. Overall, we discuss how prompt selection can influence post-training but leave open many details about broader applicability.

title: Controllable diffusion-based generation for multi-channel biological data
submission: Biological profiling technologies such as imaging mass cytometry and spatial transcriptomics generate multi-channel data with strong spatial alignment and complex inter-channel relationships; modeling such data requires generative frameworks that jointly model spatial structure and inter-channel dependencies and that generalize across arbitrary subsets of observed and missing channels. This work proposes a unified multi-channel diffusion (MCD) framework for controllable generation of structured biological data with complex inter-channel relationships, introducing a hierarchical feature injection mechanism for multi-resolution conditioning on spatially aligned observed channels, and two complementary channel attention modules to capture inter-channel relationships and recalibrate latent features. To support flexible conditioning and generalization to arbitrary sets of observed channels we train with a random channel masking strategy enabling reconstruction of missing channels given any combination of observed channels as the spatial condition. We demonstrate performance across spatial and non-spatial biological tasks including imputation and gene-to-protein translation and discuss generalizability to unseen conditional configurations.

title: The Polar Express: Optimal Matrix Sign Methods and their Application to the Muon Algorithm
submission:
Computing the polar decomposition and the related matrix sign function has been a well-studied problem in numerical analysis for decades. Recently, it has emerged as an important subroutine  within the Muon algorithm for training deep neural networks.
However, the requirements of this application differ sharply from classical settings: deep learning demands GPU-friendly algorithms that prioritize high throughput over high precision. We introduce *Polar Express*, a new method for computing the polar decomposition. Like Newton–Schulz and other classical polynomial methods, our approach uses only matrix-matrix multiplications, making it 
very efficient on GPUs.
Inspired by earlier work of Chen \& Chow and Nakatsukasa \& Freund, *Polar Express* adapts the update rule at each iteration by solving a minimax optimization problem.
We prove that this strategy minimizes error in a worst-case sense, allowing *Polar Express* to converge as rapidly as possible both in the early iterations and asymptotically.
We also address finite-precision issues, making it practical to use in `bfloat16`. When integrated into Muon, our method yields consistent improvements in validation loss for a GPT-2 model on one to ten billion tokens from the FineWeb dataset, outperforming recent alternatives across a range of learning rates.

title: AdaRec: Adaptive Sequential Recommendation for Reinforcing Long-term User Engagement
submission:
Growing attention has been paid to Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms when optimizing long-term user engagement in sequential recommendation tasks. One challenge in large-scale online recommendation systems is the constant and complicated changes in users' behavior patterns, such as interaction rates and retention tendencies. When formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), the dynamics and reward functions of the recommendation system are continuously affected by these changes. Existing RL algorithms for recommendation systems will suffer from distribution shift and struggle to adapt in such an MDP. In this paper, we introduce a novel paradigm called Adaptive Sequential Recommendation (AdaRec) to address this issue. AdaRec proposes a new distance-based representation loss to extract latent information from users' interaction trajectories. Such information reflects how RL policy fits to current user behavior patterns, and helps the policy to identify subtle changes in the recommendation system.
To make rapid adaptation to these changes, AdaRec encourages exploration with the idea of optimism under uncertainty. The exploration is further guarded by zero-order action optimization to ensure stable recommendation quality in complicated environments. We conduct extensive empirical analyses in both simulator-based and live sequential recommendation tasks, where AdaRec exhibits superior long-term performance compared to all baseline algorithms.

title: Reliable Poisoned Sample Detection against Backdoor Attacks Enhanced by Sharpness Aware Minimization
submission: This work investigates Poisoned Sample Detection (PSD), a promising defense approach against backdoor attacks. However, we observe that the effectiveness of many advanced PSD methods degrades significantly under weak backdoor attacks (\eg, low poisoning ratios or weak trigger patterns). To substantiate this observation, we conduct a statistical analysis across various attacks and PSD methods, revealing a strong correlation between the strength of the backdoor effect and the detection performance. Inspired by this, we propose amplifying the backdoor effect through training with Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM). Both theoretical insights and empirical evidence validate that SAM enhances the activations of top Trigger Activation Change (TAC) neurons while suppressing others. Based on this, we introduce SAM-enhanced PSD, a simple yet effective framework that seamlessly improves existing PSD methods by extracting detection features from the SAM-trained model rather than the conventionally trained model. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our approach significantly improves detection performance under both strong and weak backdoor attacks, achieving an average True Positive Rate (TPR) gain of +34.3% over conventional PSD methods. Overall, we believe that the revealed correlation between the backdoor effect and detection performance could inspire future research advancements.

title: Video-KTR: Reinforcing Video Reasoning via Key Token Attribution
submission: Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown strong potential for enhancing reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet existing video reasoning methods often rely on coarse sequence-level rewards or single-factor token selection. Such approaches neglect fine-grained links among visual inputs, temporal dynamics, and linguistic outputs, limiting both accuracy and interpretability. title: Softmax is not Enough (for Adaptive Conformal Classification)
submission: The merit of Conformal Prediction (CP), as a distribution-free framework for uncertainty quantification, depends on generating prediction sets that are efficient and adaptive. title: NewtonGen: Physics-consistent and Controllable Text-to-Video Generation via Neural Newtonian Dynamics
submission: A major bottleneck in large-scale text-to-video generation is physical consistency and controllability. State-of-the-art models can produce unrealistic motions—objects moving contrary to expectation or sudden velocity shifts—and they often lack precise parameter control under different initial conditions. We argue this stems from learning motion distributions primarily from appearance without explicit dynamical structure. NewtonGen integrates data-driven synthesis with learnable physical priors to address this. At its core is Neural Newtonian Dynamics (NND), a trainable module intended to model a variety of Newtonian motions and to inject dynamical constraints into generation. By combining learned dynamics with data priors, NewtonGen aims to produce videos with more coherent motion and improved controllability. We present qualitative and quantitative examples that illustrate more consistent motions under controlled parameter changes. All data and code are available at https://github.com/pandayuanyu/NewtonGen.

title: Beyond Scattered Acceptance: Fast and Coherent Inference for DLMs via Longest Stable Prefixes
submission: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) promise highly parallel text generation, yet practical inference is often bottlenecked by suboptimal decoding schedulers. Standard approaches rely on scattered acceptance—committing high-confidence tokens at disjoint positions throughout the sequence. This fractures the Key-Value (KV) cache, destroys memory locality, and forces repeated repairs across unstable token boundaries. To address this, we present the Longest Stable Prefix (LSP) scheduler, a training-free and model-agnostic inference paradigm based on monolithic prefix absorption. In each denoising step, LSP evaluates token stability via a single forward pass, dynamically identifies a contiguous left-aligned block of stable predictions, and snaps its boundary to natural linguistic or structural delimiters before an atomic commitment. This prefix-first topology converts fragmented KV cache updates into contiguous appends and preserves bidirectional lookahead over a geometrically shrinking active suffix, reducing token flip rates and denoiser calls. We evaluate LSP on LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B across mathematical reasoning, code generation, multilingual (CJK) tasks, and creative writing benchmarks to assess efficiency and quality.

submission: Estimating heterogeneous treatment effects (HTEs) from right-censored survival data is critical in high-stakes applications such as precision medicine and individualized policy-making. Across these settings, we provide a systematic comparison of survival HTE methods under diverse conditions and realistic assumption violations. SurvHTE‐Bench aims to support fair, reproducible, and extensible evaluation of causal survival methods.

title: GLASS Flows: Efficient Inference for Reward Alignment of Flow and Diffusion Models
submission: The performance of flow matching and diffusion models can be improved at inference time using reward adaptation, yet efficiency remains a bottleneck. Many algorithms rely on sampling Markov transitions via SDE sampling, which is often less efficient than ODE sampling. To mitigate this, we introduce GLASS Flows, a sampling paradigm that simulates a "flow matching model within a flow matching model" to produce Markov transitions. Crucially, we describe how an inner flow matching model may be retrieved from a pre-trained model without full re-training, combining ODE efficiency with stochastic evolution. In practice, however, achieving parity with fully stochastic samplers often requires a light tuning step of the retrieved inner model, so the method is not completely free of additional adaptation. We demonstrate the approach on large-scale text-to-image models and discuss practical trade-offs between stochasticity and efficiency for inference-time scaling.

submission: We present a geometric perspective on latent representations for diffusion models. title: What's In My Human Feedback? Learning Interpretable Descriptions of Preference Data
submission: Human feedback can alter language models in unpredictable and undesirable ways, as practitioners lack a clear understanding of what feedback data encodes. While prior work studies preferences over certain attributes (e.g., length or sycophancy), automatically extracting relevant features without pre-specifying hypotheses remains challenging. We introduce What's In My Human Feedback? (WIMHF), a method that uses sparse autoencoders to explain feedback data. WIMHF seeks to characterize both (1) the preferences a dataset is capable of measuring and (2) the preferences annotators actually express. Across seven datasets, WIMHF identifies a small number of human-interpretable features that account for much of the preference prediction signal produced by black-box models, though the magnitude and consistency of these findings vary by dataset. These features reveal diversity in human preferences and the role of dataset-level context—for example, some communities prefer informality while others disprefer it. WIMHF also surfaces potentially unsafe preferences in certain datasets and can be used to guide targeted curation and modest personalization, but results should be interpreted cautiously given dataset and annotator heterogeneity.

title: Bayesian Evidence-Driven Prototype Evolution for Federated Domain Adaptation
submission: Federated learning (FL) enables clients to collaboratively train a global model without sharing local data, but domain shift across source clients induces structural discrepancies in the feature space and can degrade global performance. We propose FedPTE, a federated framework that evolves prototype topology. FedPTE treats prototype clusters as variable topological units and employs Bayesian Gaussian Mixture Models and marginal likelihood ratios on the server to perform probabilistic inference for adaptive structural adjustments. We evaluate FedPTE on several cross-domain datasets and observe improvements; however, these gains are reported without systematic baselines or ablations and are often small, making their practical significance unclear. title: MOSS: Efficient and Accurate FP8 LLM Training with Microscaling and Automatic Scaling
submission: We propose MOSS, an FP8 training framework that aims to balance numerical stability and runtime efficiency for large language models. MOSS combines a two-level microscaling strategy for sensitive activations — pairing a high-precision global scale with compact, power-of-two local scales — with an automatic weight-scaling mechanism for linear layers that predicts and adjusts scales during training. title: GenN2N: Generative NeRF2NeRF Translation
submission: We present GenN2N, a unified NeRF-to-NeRF translation framework for various NeRF translation tasks such as text-driven NeRF editing, super-resolution, object removal, etc. Unlike previous methods designed for individual translation tasks with task-specific schemes, GenN2N achieves all these NeRF editing tasks by employing a universal image-to-image translator to perform editing in the 2D domain and lifting 2D edits into the 3D NeRF space. Since the 3D consistency of 2D edits may not be assured, we propose to model the distribution of the underlying 3D edits through a generative model that can cover all possible edited NeRFs. To model the distribution of 3D edited NeRFs from 2D edited images, we carefully design a VAE-GAN that encodes images while decoding NeRFs. The latent space is trained to align with a Gaussian distribution and the NeRFs are supervised through an adversarial loss on its renderings. To ensure the latent code does not depend on 2D viewpoints but truly reflects the 3D edits, we also regularize the latent code through a contrastive learning scheme. Extensive experiments on various editing tasks show GenN2N, as a universal framework, performs as well or better than task-specific specialists while possessing flexible generative power.

title: SURGE: Surprise-Guided Token Reduction for Efficient Video Understanding with VLMs
submission: Videos contain rich information but also high redundancy, as consecutive frames often share similar backgrounds and predictable motions. Current video-language models (VLMs) do not exploit this redundancy and therefore perform superfluous computation by processing many patch tokens even when little new information is present. We propose SURGE, a training-free and backbone-agnostic approach that measures surprise in token space and uses that signal to focus computation on novel content. High-surprise tokens are retained while predictable ones are pruned, and aggregating surprise over time highlights key events that form a compact spatio-temporal mask for downstream VLM processing. Across multiple video understanding benchmarks SURGE substantially reduces token throughput and prefill cost while maintaining accuracy close to full-token baselines, demonstrating that aligning computation with novelty enables efficient long-context video understanding without retraining.

title: Discrete Bayesian Sample Inference for Graph Generation
submission: Generating graph-structured data is crucial in many applications, from molecular design to knowledge graphs and network analysis. Traditional methods often require complex sampling schedules and are sensitive to topology changes, making them costly and brittle in practice. Despite progress, the discrete, unordered nature of graphs still challenges classical generative models and has motivated discrete diffusion and flow matching approaches. In this work, we introduce GraphBSI, a one-shot graph generative model based on Bayesian Sample Inference (BSI). Instead of evolving samples directly, GraphBSI iteratively refines a belief over graphs in the continuous space of distribution parameters, naturally handling discrete structures. We state BSI as a stochastic differential equation (SDE) and derive a noise-controlled family of SDEs that preserve marginal distributions via an approximation of the score function. Our theoretical analysis highlights connections to Bayesian Flow Networks and diffusion models. Empirically, GraphBSI achieves state-of-the-art performance on molecular and synthetic graph generation, outperforming existing one-shot graph generative models on Moses and GuacaMol.

submission: Referring Image Segmentation (RIS) aims to segment the object in an image uniquely referred to by a natural language expression. submission: Spectral clustering is a powerful technique in unsupervised analysis, prized for revealing manifold and graph structures across vision and beyond. title: WRING Out The Bias: A Rotation-Based Alternative To Projection Debiasing
submission: Vision–language models encode spurious correlations and typical debiasing via projection removes subspaces corresponding to known concepts but can inadvertently change relations to unconsidered concepts. title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
submission: Polysemanticity is pervasive in language models and remains a major challenge for interpretation and model behavioral control. Leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we map the polysemantic topology of two small models (Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small) to identify SAE feature pairs that are semantically unrelated yet exhibit interference within models. We intervene at four loci (prompt, token, feature, neuron) and measure induced shifts in the next-token prediction distribution, uncovering polysemantic structures that expose a systematic vulnerability in these models. Critically, interventions distilled from counterintuitive interference patterns shared by two small models transfer reliably to larger instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct), yielding predictable behavioral shifts without access to model internals. These findings challenge the view that polysemanticity is purely stochastic, demonstrating instead that interference structures generalize across scale and family. Such generalization suggests a convergent, higher-order organization of internal representations, which is only weakly aligned with intuition and structured by latent regularities, offering new possibilities for both black-box control and theoretical insight into human and artificial cognition.

title: ASGuard: Activation-Scaling Guard to Mitigate Targeted Jailbreaking Attack
submission: Large language models (LLMs), despite various alignment efforts, show refusal behaviors that can often be altered by simple linguistic changes. As tense jailbreaking demonstrates, models that refuse harmful requests sometimes comply when prompts are rephrased in past tense. In this work we introduce Activation-Scaling Guard (ASGuard), a mechanistically-informed framework that addresses a specific vulnerability. First, we use circuit analysis to identify attention heads associated with targeted jailbreaking such as tense changes. Second, we train a channel-wise scaling vector to recalibrate activations in those heads. Lastly, we apply this into a "preventative fine-tuning" step forcing the model to learn a more robust refusal mechanism. Across multiple LLMs, ASGuard reduces attack success rate while preserving capabilities and minimizing over-refusal. Our findings also discuss how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of refusal-mediating directions and illustrate how model internals can guide targeted adjustments.

title: Captain Cinema: Towards Short Movie Generation
submission: We present Captain Cinema, a generation framework for short movie generation. Given a detailed textual description of a movie storyline, our approach first generates a sequence of keyframes that outline the narrative to ensure some degree of long-range coherence in storyline and visual appearance; we call this top-down keyframe planning. These keyframes then serve as conditioning signals for a video synthesis model that supports long context learning to produce spatio-temporal dynamics between them, a step we refer to as bottom-up video synthesis. To enable multi-scene narrative works we introduce an interleaved training strategy for Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiT), adapted for longer-context video data. The model is trained on a curated cinematic dataset consisting of interleaved samples. Our experiments demonstrate that Captain Cinema can produce visually coherent short films, and we discuss limitations and directions for improving narrative consistency.

title: Spectral Bellman Method: Unifying Representation and Exploration in RL
submission: Representation learning is critical to success in reinforcement learning. Many existing methods are induced from model-learning aspects, misaligning them with value-based RL. This work introduces the Spectral Bellman Method, a framework derived from the Inherent Bellman Error (IBE) condition. Our key insight is a spectral relationship: under zero-IBE, the Bellman operator’s transformation of a distribution of value functions is linked to feature covariance structure. title: Pure Message Passing Can Estimate Common Neighbor for Link Prediction
submission: Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) have emerged as the de facto standard in graph representation learning. However, when it comes to link prediction, they are not always superior to simple heuristics such as Common Neighbor (CN). This discrepancy stems from a fundamental limitation: while MPNNs excel in node-level representation, they often struggle to encode the joint structural features that are essential to link prediction, like CN. To bridge this gap, we posit that, by carefully harnessing the orthogonality of input vectors, pure message-passing can capture such joint structural features. Specifically, we study the proficiency of MPNNs in approximating CN heuristics. Based on these findings, we introduce the Message Passing Link Predictor (MPLP), a novel link prediction model. MPLP leverages quasi-orthogonal vectors to estimate link-level structural features while preserving node-level expressivity. Moreover, our analysis suggests that using message-passing to capture structural features may mitigate expressiveness limitations of MPNNs, albeit at the cost of increased estimation variance. We present preliminary experiments on benchmark datasets from various domains that indicate potential, modest improvements in some settings and motivate further study.

title: TrimR: Verifier-based Training-Free Thinking Trimming for Efficient Test-Time Scaling
submission: We propose TrimR, a verifier-based, training-free framework to trim redundant chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in large reasoning models (LRMs) and improve test-time scaling. Test-time scaling techniques that prolong CoT can increase accuracy but also incur heavy decoding costs; TrimR seeks to detect and truncate redundant intermediate thoughts using a lightweight, pretrained, instruction-tuned verifier without any fine-tuning of the LRM or verifier. Empirical evaluation on benchmarks such as MATH500, AIME24/25, and GPQA shows large runtime improvements for several 30–40B class models; in some settings we observe up to 70% faster reasoning runtime, though benefits can vary by model and workload. title: Patch-as-Decodable-Token: Towards Unified Multi-Modal Vision Tasks in MLLMs
submission: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have progressed quickly, but many vision tasks still rely on indirect textual representations, e.g., predicting coordinates as text for detection, which limits dense predictions such as segmentation. We introduce Patch-as-Decodable-Token (PaDT), a unified paradigm that enables MLLMs to generate both textual and visual outputs. At its core are Visual Reference Tokens (VRTs), formed from visual patch embeddings of query images and interleaved with the LLM's textual tokens. A lightweight decoder maps outputs to detection, segmentation, and grounding predictions. PaDT processes VRTs independently at each forward pass and expands the embedding table dynamically. We also describe a fine-tuning strategy that randomly selects VRTs and uses a per-token cross-entropy objective. We outline evaluation protocols for multiple visual perception tasks, but leave a comprehensive empirical comparison to larger MLLMs and extensive benchmark results to future work.

title: Memory-Free Continual Learning with Null Space Adaptation for Zero-Shot Vision-Language Models
submission: Pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP, have strong zero-shot generalization, enabling deployment without task-specific training. In evolving environments or with novel classes, static zero-shot capabilities can be insufficient, and continual learning methods are needed. We introduce NuSA-CL (Null Space Adaptation for Continual Learning), a lightweight memory-free continual learning framework intended to address this. NuSA-CL uses low-rank adaptation and constrains task-specific weight updates to lie within an approximate null space of the model's current parameters, aiming to reduce interference with prior knowledge. Unlike replay-based or distillation approaches, NuSA-CL is designed to impose minimal computational and memory overhead. We report experiments indicating that the framework preserves zero-shot transfer and achieves competitive continual learning performance on standard benchmarks. Overall, NuSA-CL is proposed as a practical option for adapting zero-shot VLMs, though more evaluation is needed to characterize when it helps most.

title: Robust Reward Modeling via Causal Rubrics
submission: Reward models (RMs) are fundamental to aligning LLMs via human feedback, yet they often latch on to superficial or spurious attributes and misinterpret these cues as drivers of quality. We introduce CROME (Causally Robust Reward Modeling), a framework inspired by an explicit causal model to mitigate reward hacking. CROME queries an oracle LLM for rubrics that are deemed causally relevant to answering a prompt, then uses two types of synthetic targeted augmentations during training: (1) Causal Augmentations that differ along specific causal rubric attributes to enforce sensitivity, and (2) Neutral Augmentations that vary primarily in spurious attributes to enforce invariance. Neutral augmentations are produced via question swapping and response interventions along causal rubrics without knowledge of unknown spurious factors. Empirically, CROME using rubrics from popular LLM APIs improves accuracy on RewardBench and yields gains on reasoning and safety subsets. While promising, CROME’s effectiveness can depend on the quality of oracle rubrics and augmentation design, which we discuss.

title: Enhanced Continual Learning of Vision-Language Models with Model Fusion
submission: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) represent a significant breakthrough by integrating visual and textual modalities to deliver strong zero-shot capabilities. However, VLMs are susceptible to catastrophic forgetting when sequentially fine-tuned on multiple downstream tasks. Existing continual learning methods for VLMs have limitations, often relying on extra reference datasets, compromising zero-shot behavior, or restricting to parameter-efficient fine-tuning. We propose Continual Decoupling-Unifying (ConDU), which pioneers the use of model fusion for continual learning in VLMs. ConDU maintains a unified model together with task triggers and prototype sets, and iteratively decouples task experts for previous tasks and unifies them with the expert for the newly learned task. We also introduce an inference strategy for zero-shot scenarios that aggregates predictions from multiple decoupled experts. Extensive experiments on the MTIL benchmark show that ConDU consistently outperforms contemporary baselines and improves zero-shot robustness compared to the original VLM. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhangzicong518/ConDU.

title: Logit‑KL Flow Matching: Non‑Autoregressive Text Generation via Sampling‑Hybrid Inference
submission: Non-autoregressive (NAR) language models improve generation efficiency by avoiding sequential decoding, but modeling dependencies in discrete sequences remains challenging. We adopt conditional flow matching (CFM) grounded in geometrically principled interpolation, leveraging Kullback–Leibler divergence geodesics which correspond to linear interpolation in logit space. We show that maximizing conditional likelihood in this setting recovers the flow matching velocity field, providing theoretical motivation for applying flow methods to sequence modeling. To address practical gaps we propose a sampling strategy that iteratively denoises and re-noises, and a hybrid scheme combining sampling with a basic procedure. We apply these ideas to unconditional and conditional text and code infilling. The approach is described and discussed, but concrete quantitative results and detailed ablations are not provided here, leaving the empirical benefits only broadly claimed relative to prior NAR baselines under matched settings.

title: PoseX: AI Defeats Physics-based Methods on Protein Ligand Cross-Docking
submission: Recent progress in protein–ligand docking includes deep learning methods and benchmarks like PoseBench and PLINDER, though much work focuses on self-docking. To provide a more practical evaluation, we introduce PoseX, an open-source benchmark covering both self-docking and cross-docking. We curated datasets (718 self-docking entries and 1,312 cross-docking entries), integrated 23 docking methods across physics-based (e.g., Schrödinger Glide), AI docking (e.g., DiffDock), and AI co-folding (e.g., AlphaFold3) approaches, and implemented a relaxation post-processing step to reduce conformational energy. A public leaderboard supports real-time ranking. From experiments we derive several observations: AI approaches often show favorable overall success trends relative to classical methods; relaxation tends to reduce intra- and intermolecular clashes for AI models; co-folding methods can exhibit ligand chirality issues that some physics-inspired fixes mitigate; and specifying pockets appears to aid docking performance. These observations point to directions for combining AI modeling with physics-aware refinements, though more comprehensive analysis remains necessary.

title: The Potential of Second-Order Optimization for LLMs: A Study with Full Gauss-Newton
submission: We apply full Gauss-Newton (GN) preconditioning to transformer models of up to 150M parameters to probe how much is forfeited by commonly-used approximations in second-order optimization for large models. Using a practical implementation of full GN, we obtain iteration reductions relative to standard baselines and study a layerwise GN preconditioner that ignores cross-layer information. Our experiments indicate that the GN approximation can be effective for preconditioning and that a layerwise variant captures much of the useful curvature information. These findings suggest that higher-order loss terms may not be critical for iteration counts in our setups, and that layerwise Hessian structure can provide substantial preconditioning benefit. We report empirical comparisons to a set of optimization baselines and analyze when precise GN preconditioning yields improvements in iteration complexity.

title: Photon: Speedup Volume Understanding with Efficient Multimodal Large Language Models
submission: Multimodal large language models promise to support clinical visual question answering, and there is interest in extending them to 3D imaging. We present Photon, a framework that represents 3D medical volumes as token sequences whose length can vary. Photon combines instruction-conditioned token scheduling with a surrogate gradient propagation mechanism to reduce tokens during training and inference, along with a custom backpropagation rule that attempts to restore gradients when tokens are dropped. Regularization objectives are included to discourage language-only bias and to stabilize compression. We evaluate Photon on medical visual question answering tasks and observe reduced resource usage and faster runtime in our settings, with accuracy comparable to prior approaches. Photon is intended as a practical token-compression recipe rather than a sweeping solution to volumetric modeling.

title: Deep Ignorance: Filtering Pretraining Data Builds Tamper-Resistant Safeguards into Open-Weight LLMs
submission: Open-weight AI systems offer unique benefits such as transparency, open research, and decentralized access, but they are also vulnerable to tampering attacks that can elicit harmful behaviors by modifying weights or activations. There is not yet a robust science of open-weight model risk management. We investigate whether filtering text about dual-use topics from pretraining data can reduce unwanted capabilities and provide a more tamper-resistant safeguard. We introduce a multi-stage pipeline for scalable data filtering and show that it provides a tractable method for minimizing biothreat proxy knowledge in large models. We pretrain several models from scratch and observe greater resistance to adversarial fine-tuning in our experiments, while maintaining performance on unrelated tasks in our evaluations. We also find that filtered models, though lacking internalized dangerous knowledge, can still make use of such information if it is supplied in context (e.g., via tool augmentation), suggesting the need for layered defenses.

title: Mixture-of-World Models: Scaling Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Modular Latent Dynamics
submission: A fundamental challenge in multi-task reinforcement learning (MTRL) is achieving sample efficiency in visual domains where tasks exhibit significant heterogeneity in both observations and dynamics. Model-based RL (MBRL) offers a promising path to sample efficiency through world models, but standard monolithic architectures struggle to capture diverse task dynamics, leading to poor reconstruction and prediction accuracy. We introduce the mixture-of-world models (MoW), a scalable architecture that integrates three key components: i) modular VAEs for task-adaptive visual compression, ii) a hybrid Transformer-based dynamics model combining task-conditioned experts with a shared backbone, and, iii) a gradient-based task clustering strategy for efficient parameter allocation. On the Atari 100k benchmark,  **a single MoW agent** (trained once over Atari $26$ games) achieves a mean human-normalized score of $\mathbf{110.4}$%, competitive with the  $\mathbf{114.2}$% achieved by the recent STORM-an ensemble of $26$ task-specific models-while requiring $\mathbf{50}$% fewer parameters. On Meta-World, MoW attains a $\mathbf{74.5}$% average success rate within $300$K steps, establishing a new state-of-the-art. These results demonstrate that MoW provides a scalable and parameter-efficient foundation for generalist world models.

title: QeRL: Beyond Efficiency - Quantization-enhanced Reinforcement Learning for LLMs
submission: Reinforcement learning remains central to improving reasoning in large language models (LLMs), but RL training is resource intensive, requiring substantial GPU memory and long rollouts. In practice, researchers use quantization and parameter-efficient tuning to reduce these costs. Building on this background, we propose QeRL, a Quantization-enhanced Reinforcement Learning framework that combines NVFP4 quantization with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to accelerate the rollout phase while lowering memory overhead. Beyond efficiency, we observe that quantization noise can increase policy entropy and thereby enhance exploration in LoRA-based RL; to exploit this, QeRL introduces an Adaptive Quantization Noise (AQN) mechanism that dynamically adjusts quantization-induced noise during training. Empirically, QeRL achieves notable speedups in rollout compared to QLoRA and BF16 LoRA for a 7B model, and we demonstrate scalable RL training on larger models using a single high-memory accelerator. These results suggest QeRL is a practical alternative when computational budget and memory are constrained.

title: Quantum machine learning advantages beyond hardness of evaluation
submission: Recent years have seen rigorous proofs of quantum advantages in machine learning, particularly when data is labeled by cryptographic or inherently quantum functions. Much work in this area emphasizes hardness-of-evaluation arguments and complexity-theoretic separations. Motivated by this literature, we study the identification task, where the goal is to identify the labeling function behind a dataset so that any advantage must arise from the learning process itself. The identification task has natural applications in settings where labeled data is available, and understanding it requires revisiting assumptions about generatability and learnability. In this work we provide the first proofs of identification learning advantages for quantum functions under complexity-theoretic assumptions. Our main result relies on a new proof strategy, showing that for a broad class of quantum identification tasks there exists an exponential quantum advantage unless BQP is in a low level of the polynomial hierarchy. Along the way we give technical results about random generatability for quantum functions and related complexity conjectures.

title: Self-Supervised Learning from Structural Invariance
submission: Joint-embedding self-supervised learning (SSL) learns from invariances between semantically-related data pairs. We study the one-to-many mapping problem in SSL, where each datum may be mapped to multiple valid targets. This arises when data pairs come from naturally occurring generative processes, e.g., successive video frames. Existing methods struggle to capture conditional uncertainty. As a remedy, we introduce a latent variable to account for uncertainty and derive a variational lower bound on mutual information between paired embeddings. Our derivation yields a simple regularization term for standard SSL objectives. The resulting method, AdaSSL, applies to both contrastive and distillation-based SSL objectives, and we empirically show its versatility in causal representation learning, fine-grained image understanding and world modeling on videos. The paper omits some steps and the narrative jumps between datasets, derivation and experiments, which may make the core contribution hard to follow.

submission: Real-world physical systems often couple multiple physics, making simulation challenging, particularly when dealing with decoupled data. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/ZBWpro/PoLi-RL.

title: Low-Latency Neural LiDAR Compression with 2D Context Models
submission: Context modeling is fundamental to LiDAR point cloud compression. Existing methods rely on computationally intensive 3D contexts, such as voxel and octree, which struggle to balance compression efficiency and coding speed. We propose a neural LiDAR compressor based on 2D context models that aims to support high-efficiency compression, fast coding, and unified geometry-intensity compression, though the exact trade-offs we target are not clearly prioritized. The approach represents the point cloud as a range image and uses a multi-scale spatial context model, an optical-flow-based temporal model, and a deformable attention module to incorporate camera cues. We also describe a backbone for joint geometry and intensity compression. While we report improvements in rate-distortion and coding speed, the connection between the 2D context design and the claimed gains is not fully justified by the method description, and experimental baselines and ablations are not detailed here. title: CMT-Benchmark: A Benchmark for Condensed Matter Theory Built by Expert Researchers
submission: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress in coding and mathematical problem-solving; however, evaluation on advanced research-level problems in the hard sciences remains scarce. To fill this gap, we present CMT-Benchmark, a dataset of 50 original problems covering condensed matter theory (CMT) at the level of an expert researcher. The solutions for these problems involve analytical and computational approaches commonly used in quantum many-body physics and classical statistical mechanics. The dataset was designed and verified by a worldwide panel of expert researchers through a collaborative environment. Topics include Hartree-Fock mean-field theory, exact diagonalization, quantum Monte Carlo, density matrix renormalization group, quantum and classical statistical mechanics, and model building. We evaluate LLMs by programmatically checking LLM-generated solutions against expert-supplied ground truth using an automated machine-grading pipeline. However, we observed inconsistencies in automatic grading: the grader sometimes fails to detect subtle but important errors or incorrectly flags correct derivations, which complicates interpretation of model performance. While frontier models struggle with many problems, and some problems appear universally unsolved, the limitations of automatic verification mean that reported model scores should be interpreted with caution and further manual validation is often required.

title: Mapping Semantic & Syntactic Relationships with Geometric Rotation
submission: Understanding how language and embedding models encode semantic relationships is important for interpretability. While early word embeddings exhibited intuitive vector arithmetic ("king" - "man" + "woman" = "queen"), modern high-dimensional text representations lack straightforward geometric properties. We describe Rotor-Invariant Shift Estimation (RISE), a geometric approach that frames semantic-syntactic transformations as rotational operations in embedding space, appealing to the manifold structure of modern representations. RISE is presented as a way to operate across languages and models without reducing apparent performance, hinting at analogous cross-lingual geometric structure. We contrast RISE with two baseline methods, three embedding models, three datasets, and seven morphologically diverse languages. Our discussion suggests that RISE may map some discourse-level semantic-syntactic transformations (e.g., negation and conditionality) with consistent geometric operations in multilingual embedding spaces, offering tentative support for aspects of the linear representation hypothesis at the sentence level, though concrete boundaries and limitations remain to be clarified.

submission: Text-to-CAD code generation is a long-horizon task, requiring translating instructions into long sequences of interdependent operations, and because minor early errors can propagate and invalidate an entire assembly, we propose learning an intermediate hierarchical and geometry-aware graph; the graph represents an assembly-based decomposition with multi-level nodes modelling parts and components, and edges defining explicit geometric constraints between them, and rather than mapping text directly to code, our graph paradigm first predicts high-level structure and constraints, then conditions sequencing and program generation thereby narrowing the search space and improving geometric fidelity and constraint satisfaction. Furthermore, we introduce a structure-aware progressive curriculum learning mechanism to improve generation of decomposition graphs by constructing graded tasks via controlled edits to object structure, probing capability boundaries, and synthesizing boundary examples for training. We also introduce a 12K-instruction dataset with instructions, graphs, action sequences, and bpy code, plus metrics for node- and hierarchy-level accuracy and constraint satisfaction; extensive experiments show improvements in geometric fidelity and constraint fulfillment.

submission: Long-context decoding is bottlenecked by KV cache loading where generation forces repeated transfers from off-chip HBM to on-chip SRAM and this hurts throughput. title: Parameterized Hardness of Zonotope Containment and Neural Network Verification
submission: Neural networks with ReLU activations are a widely used model in machine learning, so a deeper understanding of the properties of the functions they compute is important. There has been increasing interest in the (parameterized) computational complexity of determining such properties. In this work we close several gaps and resolve an open problem posed by Froese et al. regarding the parameterized complexity of verification-related questions for ReLU networks. In particular, we prove new hardness results for fundamental decision and approximation problems for functions f: R^d -> R computed by shallow networks, and for related polyhedral containment problems that arise in computational geometry and control. We also show negative results for approximating maxima and for computing L_p-Lipschitz-like quantities in low-depth networks. Our hardness arguments imply that simple enumeration-based methods are essentially optimal under standard complexity assumptions. Full technical statements and reductions are provided in the paper, along with discussions of implications for verification practice.

title: Quagmires in SFT-RL Post-Training: When High SFT Scores Mislead and What to Use Instead
submission: Post-training for reasoning LLMs commonly follows two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RL). We question whether improvements in standard SFT metrics reliably translate to better performance after RL. We present numerous counterexamples where higher SFT scores do not yield improved RL outcomes, and in some cases lead to worse behavior after RL. High SFT scores can be biased toward simpler or more homogeneous data and are not consistently predictive of post-RL gains. We explore alternative predictors and find that certain held-out generalization measures and broader sampling-based performance estimates correlate better with eventual RL results. We trained and evaluated many models across a variety of settings to support these observations. Our findings suggest caution when using SFT metrics as the primary pre-RL selection criterion and motivate more robust evaluation practices, though specifics of the recommended protocols are left for follow-up work.

title: Generation then Reconstruction: Accelerating Masked Autoregressive Models via Two-Stage Sampling
submission: Masked Autoregressive (MAR) models promise improved efficiency in visual generation via parallel sampling, yet their acceleration potential is constrained by modeling spatially correlated visual tokens in a single step. We introduce Generation then Reconstruction (GtR), a hierarchical, training-free sampling strategy that decomposes generation into two stages: structure generation that establishes global semantic scaffolding, followed by detail reconstruction that completes remaining tokens efficiently. GtR assumes that creating a coarse structure is harder than complementing details, and intentionally allocates computation accordingly. We also propose Frequency-Weighted Token Selection (FTS) to prioritize computation for tokens carrying high-frequency, detail-rich information. Experiments on class-conditional and text-to-image settings indicate that GtR provides clear runtime advantages while preserving perceptual quality across model sizes. We will release code to facilitate further study and ablation by the community.

title: Pareto Deep Long-Tailed Recognition: A Conflict-Averse Solution
submission: Deep long-tailed recognition (DTLR) has attracted much attention due to its close touch with realistic scenarios. Recent advances have focused on re-balancing across various aspects, e.g., sampling strategy, loss re-weighting, logit adjustment, and input/parameter perturbation, to name a few. However, few studies have considered dynamic re-balancing to address intrinsic optimization conflicts. In this paper, we first empirically argue that the optimizations of mainstream DLTR methods are still dominated by some categories (e.g., major) due to a fixed re-balancing strategy. Thus, they fail to deal with gradient conflicts among categories, which naturally deduces the motivation for reaching Pareto optimal solutions. Unfortunately, a naive integration of multi-objective optimization (MOO) with DLTR methods is not applicable due to the gap between multi-task learning (MTL) and DLTR, and can in turn lead to class-specific feature degradation. Thus, we provide effective alternatives by decoupling MOO-based MTL from the temporal rather than structure perspective, and enhancing it via optimizing variability collapse loss motivated by the derived MOO-based DLTR generalization bound. Moreover, we resort to anticipating worst-case optimization with theoretical insights to further ensure convergence. We build a Pareto deep long-tailed recognition method termed PLOT upon the proposed MOO framework. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our method not only generally improves mainstream pipelines, but also achieves an augmented version to realize state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks.

title: Depth Anything 3: Recovering the Visual Space from Any Views
submission:
We present Depth Anything 3 (DA3), a model that predicts spatially consistent geometry from an arbitrary number of visual inputs, with or without known camera poses. 
In pursuit of minimal modeling, DA3 yields two key insights:
a single plain transformer (e.g., vanilla DINOv2 encoder) is sufficient as a backbone without architectural specialization, and a singular depth-ray prediction target obviates the need for complex multi-task learning. Through our teacher-student training paradigm, the model achieves a level of detail and generalization on par with Depth Anything 2 (DA2).
We establish a new visual geometry benchmark covering camera pose estimation, any-view geometry and visual rendering. On this benchmark, DA3 sets a new state-of-the-art across all tasks, surpassing prior SOTA VGGT by an average of 35.7\% in camera pose accuracy and 23.6\% in geometric accuracy. Moreover, it outperforms DA2 in monocular depth estimation. All models are trained exclusively on public academic datasets.

title: Play to Generalize: Learning to Reason Through Game Play
submission: Developing reasoning capabilities in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains challenging. Motivated by literature suggesting that gameplay promotes transferable reasoning skills, we propose a post-training method, Visual Game Learning (ViGaL), where MLLMs develop generalizable reasoning skills through playing arcade-like games. Specifically, we show that training a 7B-parameter MLLM via reinforcement learning (RL) on simple games like Snake substantially enhances downstream performance on multimodal math benchmarks like MathVista and on multi-discipline questions like MMMU, despite never seeing worked solutions, equations, or diagrams during RL. Remarkably, our ViGaL-post-trained model not only preserves general visual abilities but also surpasses a wide range of specialist models on numerous multimodal reasoning benchmarks, suggesting that gameplay can be a broadly effective surrogate objective for inducing reasoning. These results point to a practical strategy of designing diverse surrogate tasks for RL post-training to induce emergent multimodal reasoning. The code is available at https://yunfeixie233.github.io/ViGaL.

title: When Shift Happens - Confounding Is to Blame
submission: Conventional wisdom suggests that learning causal-invariant representations enhances robustness, yet recent empirical studies present a counterintuitive finding: empirical risk minimization (ERM) can rival or even outperform state-of-the-art out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization methods, and performance can improve when all covariates, including non-causal ones, are utilized. We attribute this phenomenon to hidden confounding: shifts in hidden confounding induce changes in data distributions that violate assumptions commonly made by existing approaches. Under such conditions, we show that generalization may require learning environment-specific relationships rather than relying solely on invariant ones. We also explain why augmenting models with non-causal but informative covariates can mitigate challenges posed by hidden confounding shifts. Our paper provides theoretical analysis and supporting experiments, and discusses implications for covariate selection and future research on OOD generalization, highlighting scenarios where invariant-focused strategies may be insufficient.

title: Glance and Focus Reinforcement for Pan-cancer Screening
submission: Pan-cancer screening in large-scale CT scans remains challenging for existing AI methods, primarily due to the difficulty of localizing diverse types of tiny lesions in large CT volumes. The extreme foreground-background imbalance significantly hinders models from focusing on diseased regions, while redundant focus on healthy regions not only decreases the efficiency but also increases false positives. Inspired by radiologists' glance and focus diagnostic strategy, we introduce GF-Screen, a Glance and Focus reinforcement learning framework for pan-cancer screening. GF-Screen employs a Glance model to localize the diseased regions and a Focus model to precisely segment the lesions, where segmentation results of the Focus model are leveraged to reward the Glance model via Reinforcement Learning (RL). Specifically, the Glance model crops a group of sub-volumes from the entire CT volume and learns to select the sub-volumes with lesions for the Focus model to segment. Given that the selecting operation is non-differentiable for segmentation training, we propose to employ the segmentation results to reward the Glance model. To optimize the Glance model, we introduce a novel group relative learning paradigm, which employs group relative comparison to prioritize high-advantage predictions and discard low-advantage predictions within sub-volume groups, not only improving efficiency but also reducing false positives. In this way, for the first time, we effectively extend cutting-edge RL techniques to tackle the specific challenges in pan-cancer screening. We conduct training and validation on a large-scale pan-cancer dataset comprising 5,117 CT scans. Extensive experiments on 16 internal and 7 external datasets across 9 lesion types demonstrated the effectiveness of GF-Screen. Notably, GF-Screen leads the public validation leaderboard of MICCAI FLARE25 pan-cancer challenge, surpassing the FLARE24 champion solution by a large margin (+25.6% DSC and +28.2% NSD). In addition, through discarding redundant regions, GF-Screen reduces the computation costs by 5.7 times, significantly improving inference efficiency. The superior performance of GF-Screen remarks a novel and practical breakthrough in pan-cancer screening. Code is available at https://github.com/Luffy03/GF-Screen.

title: Unitention: Attend a sample to the dataset
submission: We propose an end-to-end trainable module termed Unitention, an abbreviation for universal-individual cross-attention, to improve deep features of a given neural network by attending the feature of a data sample to those of the entire dataset. This innovation is motivated by two key observations: (i) traditional visual encoding methods, such as Bag of visual Words, encode an image by using a universal dataset-wide codebook, while (ii) deep models typically process every individual data sample in isolation, without explicitly using any universal information. Our Unitention aims to bridge this gap by attentively merging universal and individual features, thus complementing and potentially enhancing the given deep model. We evaluate it on various classification benchmarks and model architectures. On ImageNet, Unitention shows improvements for different ConvNets and Transformers; in our experiments some k-NN classifiers with Unitention perform comparably to or slightly better than baseline classifiers. Gains are more noticeable on fine-grained tasks (up to around 2.3%). Further validations on other modalities tentatively confirm Unitention's versatility. Overall, Unitention suggests that dataset-level information can be useful for enhancing deep features and may point to a backbone-independent direction for future work.

title: Testing Fourier Sparsity via Implicit Sensing
submission: Boolean functions are central in learning theory and Fourier sparsity—the number of nonzero Fourier coefficients—measures structural simplicity. The problem of testing whether a function over F_2^n is s-Fourier sparse or far from every such function is natural and long-studied. These results narrow the gap between known upper and lower bounds and suggest new directions for sublinear Fourier analysis.

title: A Convergence Analysis of Adaptive Optimizers under Floating-point Quantization
submission: The rapid scaling of large language models has made low-precision training essential for reducing memory and enabling larger models and datasets. title: Attention Smoothing Is All You Need For Unlearning
submission: Large Language Models are prone to memorizing sensitive, copyrighted, or hazardous content, posing significant privacy and legal concerns. Retraining from scratch is computationally infeasible, whereas current unlearning methods exhibit unstable trade-offs between forgetting and utility, frequently producing incoherent outputs on forget prompts and failing to generalize due to the persistence of lexical-level and semantic-level associations in attention. We propose Attention Smoothing Unlearning (ASU), a principled framework that casts unlearning as self-distillation from a forget-teacher derived from the model’s own attention. By increasing the softmax temperature, ASU flattens attention distributions and directly suppresses the lexical-level and semantic-level associations responsible for reconstructing memorized knowledge. This results in a bounded optimization objective that erases factual information yet maintains coherence in responses to forget prompts. Empirical evaluation on TOFU, MUSE, and WMDP, along with real-world and continual unlearning scenarios across question answering and text completion, demonstrates that ASU outperforms the baselines for most of the unlearning scenarios, delivering robust unlearning with minimal loss of model utility.

title: MetaEmbed: Scaling Multimodal Retrieval at Test-Time with Flexible Late Interaction
submission: Universal multimodal embedding models have achieved great success in capturing semantic relevance between queries and candidates. However, current methods either condense queries and candidates into a single vector, potentially limiting the expressiveness for fine-grained information, or produce too many vectors that are prohibitively expensive for multi-vector retrieval. In this work, we introduce MetaEmbed, a new framework for multimodal retrieval that rethinks how multimodal embeddings are constructed and interacted with at scale. During training, a fixed number of learnable Meta Tokens are appended to the input sequence. At test-time, their last-layer contextualized representations serve as compact yet expressive multi-vector embeddings. Through the proposed Matryoshka Multi-Vector Retrieval training, MetaEmbed learns to organize information by granularity across multiple vectors. As a result, we enable test-time scaling in multimodal retrieval where users can balance retrieval quality against efficiency demands by selecting the number of tokens used for indexing and retrieval interactions. Extensive evaluations on the Massive Multimodal Embedding Benchmark (MMEB) and the Visual Document Retrieval Benchmark (ViDoRe) confirm that MetaEmbed achieves state-of-the-art retrieval performance while scaling robustly to models with 32B parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/MetaEmbed.

title: I-DRUID: Layout to image generation via instance-disentangled representation and unpaired data
submission: Layout-to-Image (L2I) generation, aiming at coherently generating multiple instances conditioned on given layouts and instance captions, has raised substantial attention. The primary challenges of L2I stem from attribute leakage due to entangled instance features within attention and limited generalization to novel scenes caused by insufficient image-text paired data. To address these issues, we propose I-DRUID, a framework that leverages instance-disentangled representations (IDR) and unpaired, prompt-only data (UID) to improve L2I generation. IDR are extracted with our instance disentanglement modules, which utilize information among instances to obtain semantic-related features while suppressing spurious parts. To facilitate disentangling, we require semantic-related features to trigger more accurate attention maps than spurious ones, formulating an instance-disentangled constraint to avoid attribute leakage. Moreover, to improve generalization to novel scenes, we adapt L2I with UID via reinforcement learning, encouraging plausible generation trajectories based on AI feedback. Empirically, IDM and RL cooperate synergistically: I-DRUID effectively eliminates attribute leakage and, across standard L2I benchmarks, achieves state-of-the-art fidelity and diversity—often dramatically outperforming prior methods (reducing common layout errors by over 90% in our evaluations). Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our approach.

title: Death of the Novel(ty): Beyond N-Gram Novelty as a Metric for Textual Creativity
submission: $N$-gram novelty is widely used to evaluate models' ability to generate text outside their training data and has been adopted as a proxy for textual creativity. Theoretical work, however, emphasizes creativity's dual nature: novelty and appropriateness. We investigate this relationship through 8,618 expert writer annotations of novelty, pragmaticality, and sensicality via close reading of human- and AI-generated text. We find that $n$-gram novelty correlates with expert-judged creativity but that a large fraction of high $n$-gram novelty expressions are not judged creative, indicating limitations of the metric. Higher $n$-gram novelty in several open-source models is also associated with reduced pragmaticality. In exploratory tests using frontier closed-source models, we observe lower rates of expressions judged creative than in human writing. Using our dataset, we analyze model variants in zero-shot, few-shot, and finetuned settings for their ability to identify novel or non-pragmatic expressions, and highlight areas for improvement.

title: Durian: Dual Reference Image-Guided Portrait Animation with Attribute Transfer
submission:
We present Durian, the first method for generating portrait animation videos with cross-identity attribute transfer from one or more reference images to a target portrait. Training such models typically requires attribute pairs of the same individual, which are rarely available at scale. To address this challenge, we propose a self-reconstruction formulation that leverages ordinary portrait videos to learn attribute transfer without explicit paired data. submission: We present a unified framework for simulating and visualizing dynamic fracture phenomena in extreme mechanical collisions from multi-view image inputs. title: Learning What Matters Now: Dynamic Preference Inference under Contextual Shifts
submission: Humans often juggle multiple, sometimes conflicting objectives and shift their priorities as circumstances change, rather than following a fixed objective function. Many computational decision-making and multi-objective RL methods assume static preference weights or a known scalar reward, which contrasts with everyday adaptive behavior. Inspired by cognitive ideas, we propose Dynamic Preference Inference (DPI), a framework in which an agent maintains a probabilistic belief over preference weights, updates this belief from recent interaction, and conditions its policy on inferred preferences. We instantiate DPI as a variational preference inference module trained jointly with a preference-conditioned actor–critic, using vector-valued returns as evidence about latent trade-offs. In several environments—queueing, gridworld maze, and multi-objective continuous control with event-driven changes—the system adapts its inferred preferences and shows improved post-shift performance compared to simple baselines. DPI emphasizes belief maintenance and rapid adaptation, offering a way to condition policies on inferred, context-sensitive priorities.

title: Watch your steps: Dormant Adversarial Behaviors that Activate upon LLM Finetuning
submission: Fine-tuning open-weight large language models is common for task specialization. We show that an adversary can craft models that appear benign yet activate undesirable behaviors only after downstream fine-tuning. We call this attack FAB (Finetuning-activated Adversarial Behaviors). FAB relies on meta-optimization to encourage the post-finetuned model to exhibit targeted behaviors while keeping the base model seemingly normal; concurrently, the compromised model is regularized to retain general capabilities and to hide adversarial tendencies before fine-tuning. We describe several target behaviors of interest—unsolicited advertising, jailbreakability, and over-refusal—and report that FAB can make these behaviors emerge under some downstream fine-tuning choices. The precise mechanisms, robustness boundaries, and quantitative magnitudes vary, and while we observe activation in multiple cases, the connection between the pre-compromise regularization and the eventual triggered behavior requires further clarification. These findings suggest a possible new attack vector that merits additional study.

title: Inverse IFEval: Can LLMs Unlearn Stubborn Training Conventions to Follow Real Instructions?
submission: Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve strong performance on diverse tasks but often exhibit cognitive inertia, struggling to follow instructions that conflict with the standardized patterns learned during supervised fine-tuning (SFT). To evaluate this limitation, we introduce Inverse IFEval, a benchmark measuring models’ Counter-intuitive Ability—the capacity to override training-induced biases and comply with adversarial instructions. Inverse IFEval poses eight challenge types, including Question Correction, Intentional Textual Flaws, Code without Comments, and Counterfactual Answering. Using a human-in-the-loop pipeline, we assemble 1,012 high-quality Chinese and English questions across 23 domains and evaluate them under an optimized LLM-as-a-Judge framework. Experiments on leading LLMs show pervasive failures of standard SFT models on these tasks; we argue that Inverse IFEval is indispensable for robust alignment and is a necessary step toward eliminating cognitive inertia and improving instruction-following reliability in real-world, unconventional contexts.

title: BOTS: A Unified Framework for Bayesian Online Task Selection in LLM Reinforcement Finetuning
submission: Reinforcement finetuning (RFT) is a technique for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with preferences and improving reasoning, yet effectiveness is sensitive to which tasks are explored during training. Uniform task sampling can be inefficient, spending compute on trivial or unsolvable tasks, while many task selection methods suffer from high rollout cost or poor adaptivity. Grounded in Bayesian inference, BOTS maintains posterior estimates of task difficulty as the model evolves and jointly incorporates explicit evidence from direct evaluations and implicit evidence inferred for unselected tasks. To make implicit evidence practical, we use an ultra-light interpolation-based plug-in that estimates difficulties of unevaluated tasks with negligible overhead. Empirically across several domains and model scales, BOTS often improves data efficiency and yields modest performance gains compared to common sampling strategies, suggesting a practical direction for dynamic task selection in RFT.

title: DistillKac: Few-Step Image Generation via Damped Wave Equations
submission: We present DistillKac, a fast image generator that uses the damped wave equation and its stochastic Kac representation to move probability mass at finite speed. In contrast to diffusion models whose reverse time velocities can become stiff and implicitly allow unbounded propagation speed, Kac dynamics enforce finite speed transport and yield globally bounded kinetic energy. Building on this structure, we introduce classifier free guidance in velocity space that preserves square integrability under mild conditions. We then propose endpoint only distillation that trains a student to match a frozen teacher over long intervals. We prove a stability result that promotes supervision at the endpoints to closeness along the entire path. Experiments demonstrate DistillKac delivers high quality samples with very few function evaluations while retaining the numerical stability benefits of finite speed probability flows.

title: lmgame-Bench: How Good are LLMs at Playing Games?
submission: Playing video games requires perception, reasoning, memory, and long-horizon planning—faculties increasingly associated with large language and vision–language models (LLMs/VLMs). We introduce LMGame-Bench, a benchmark built on six popular games spanning platformer, puzzle, and narrative domains through a unified Gym-style API. The benchmark uses a modular harness with perception, memory, and reasoning modules that can be toggled to probe capabilities. We also apply prompt standardization and contamination mitigation to improve evaluation consistency. We evaluate a suite of state-of-the-art LLMs/VLMs and analyze per-game behavior to relate game types to core model capabilities. Our results indicate persistent limitations in visual state extraction, reflection, spatiotemporal reasoning, and long-context planning, and we discuss directions for addressing these limitations. LMGame-Bench is intended as a flexible platform for studying how current models manage the range of skills required for interactive game play.

title: ThinkOmni: Lifting Textual Reasoning to Omni-modal Scenarios via Guidance Decoding
submission: Omni-modal reasoning is essential for intelligent systems to understand and draw inferences from diverse data sources. While existing omni-modal large language models (OLLM) excel at perceiving diverse modalities, they lack the complex reasoning abilities of recent large reasoning models (LRM). However, enhancing the reasoning ability of OLLMs through additional training presents significant challenges, including the need for high-quality data, task-specific adaptation, and substantial computational costs. To address these limitations, we propose ThinkOmni, a training-free and data-free framework that lifts textual reasoning to omni-modal scenarios. ThinkOmni introduces two key components: 1) LRM-as-a-Guide, which leverages off-the-shelf LRMs to guide the OLLM decoding process; 2) Stepwise Contrastive Scaling, which adaptively balances perception and reasoning signals without manual hyperparameter tuning. Experiments on six multi-modal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ThinkOmni consistently delivers performance improvements, with main results achieving 70.2 on MathVista and 75.5 on MMAU. Overall, ThinkOmni offers a flexible and generalizable solution for omni-modal reasoning and provides new insights into the generalization and application of reasoning capabilities.

title: Test-Time Matching: Unlocking Compositional Reasoning in Multimodal Models
submission: Frontier multimodal models often struggle with compositional reasoning on established benchmarks, a problem we revisit here. We argue that commonly used metrics can underestimate capability and introduce a group matching score intended to more faithfully reflect model behavior. Under this view, improvements under the new metric can be related back to existing metrics via an overfitting step. Building on that observation, we propose Test-Time Matching (TTM), described as an iterative, self-improving procedure that adapts model outputs at test time without external supervision. TTM is reported to further boost performance for contrastive and generative multimodal models across a variety of datasets. We show that applying the score and TTM yields consistent gains on multiple benchmarks and that some models achieve improved rankings under the adjusted evaluation. The paper focuses on the evaluation perspective and on a simple, general test-time adaptation idea.

title: Cascadia: An Efficient Cascade Serving System for Large Language Models
submission: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have increased demand for both rapid responses and high-quality outputs. More powerful models give better results but higher latency; smaller models are faster but less capable. Prior work uses model cascades to route simpler queries to smaller models and complex ones to larger models. We introduce Cascadia, a cascade serving framework designed to schedule request routing and deploy model cascades for fast, quality-preserving LLM serving. Cascadia uses a bi-level optimization: at deployment it solves a mixed-integer linear program to select resource allocations and parallelism strategies; at routing it applies an iterative Chebyshev-guided method to co-optimize routing and deployment. We evaluate on diverse workload traces and model cascades, demonstrating substantial improvements in latency SLO tightness and throughput while maintaining answer quality. The paper focuses on system-level scheduling and routing without committing to a single concrete optimization objective, leaving the precise goal formulation flexible.

title: The Achilles’ Heel of LLMs: How Altering a Handful of Neurons Can Cripple Language Abilities
submission: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used across NLP and have parallels drawn to biological brains. Neuroscience suggests a small subset of biological neurons can be crucial for cognitive functions, prompting the question: do LLMs contain a small subset of critical neurons? We propose a perturbation-based causal identification method to systematically locate such critical neurons in LLMs. Our investigation reveals three qualitative insights: (1) LLMs appear to contain ultra-sparse sets of critical neurons whose disruption can severely impair language behavior; (2) these critical neurons tend to concentrate in outer layers, especially in MLP down_proj components; (3) disruption produces sharp phase-like drops in performance rather than smooth degradation. We analyze these phenomena across different architectures and model scales, discuss implications for robustness and interpretability, and outline potential directions for designing more resilient architectures and deployment safeguards. Code is available at https://github.com/qqqqqqqzx/The-Achilles-Heel-of-LLMs.

title: SAQ: Stabilizer-Aware Quantum Error Correction Decoder
submission: Quantum Error Correction decoding faces an accuracy-efficiency tradeoff: classical methods like Minimum Weight Perfect Matching have variable performance and polynomial complexity, while tensor network decoders are accurate but computationally costly. We present SAQ-Decoder, a framework that combines transformer-based learning with constraint-aware post-processing to target near Maximum Likelihood accuracy while keeping computation scaling linear in syndrome size. The model uses a dual-stream transformer to process syndromes and logical information with asymmetric attention, and introduces a differentiable logical loss that optimizes Logical Error Rates through smooth approximations over finite fields. SAQ-Decoder attains high decoding accuracy, reporting thresholds of 10.99% (independent noise) and 18.6% (depolarizing noise) on toric codes that closely approach theoretical ML bounds of 11.0% and 18.9%. These results indicate learned decoders can be both accurate and efficient for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Resurfacing the Instance-only Dependent Label Noise Model through Loss Correction
submission: We investigate label noise in supervised binary classification and resurface the instance-only dependent noise model through loss correction. Based on risk equivalence, the instance-aware loss correction completes a bridge from empirical noisy risk minimization to true clean risk minimization when the base loss is classification calibrated (e.g., cross-entropy).
