Empirical findings over different dataset domains (image, audio, tabular) with different learners (neural networks, gradient-boosted machines) validate the generalization ability of the method. The method can be applied in practice and is broadly useful. Future directions include more robust estimators and extensions to multiclass settings.

title: Efficient Quantization of Mixture-of-Experts with Theoretical Generalization Guarantees
submission: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) enables efficient scaling by activating only a subset of experts per input, but the large parameter count still causes substantial memory overhead at inference. Post-training quantization is a promising remedy; uniform quantization degrades accuracy at low bit-widths, and recent mixed-precision schemes aim to address this. We propose a theoretically grounded expert-wise mixed-precision strategy that allocates precision per expert to better preserve model performance while reducing inference cost. Our approach is motivated by the observation that different experts have different impact on final accuracy and therefore should receive different precision budgets. We also introduce simple criteria to avoid assigning low precision to highly sensitive experts. Experiments on large-scale MoE models including Switch Transformer and Mixtral show that our method yields higher accuracy than several existing approaches while reducing inference cost and incurring only small overhead for bit-width assignment. We provide analysis that supports the practicality of the scheme and discuss deployment considerations.

title: Sequential Information Bottleneck Fusion: Towards Robust and Generalizable Multi-Modal Brain Tumor Segmentation
submission: Brain tumor segmentation in multi-modal MRI is difficult when modalities are missing. We advocate sequential information bottleneck fusion to better preserve shared information across modalities, arguing from an information-theoretic perspective that sequential fusion can yield more robust fused representations and a tighter generalization bound than parallel fusion. Based on this, we propose the Sequential Multi-modal Segmentation Network (SMSN) which integrates an Information-Bottleneck Fusion Module (IBFM) that sequentially extracts modality-common features while reconstructing modality-specific ones via a dedicated extractor. We report experiments on BRATS18 and BRATS20 and describe transfer attempts to a brain metastasis dataset. Results indicate some robustness in missing-modality settings, though direct comparisons to many established parallel-fusion baselines are limited in this work. We provide architectural and training details in the supplement to facilitate follow-up studies.

submission: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a powerful approach for black-box optimization. title: Kevin: Multi-Turn RL for Generating CUDA Kernels
submission: Writing GPU kernels is iterative: domain experts write code and improve performance through execution feedback, and the process includes verifiable signals like correctness and speed. We develop a flexible multi-turn RL recipe that attempts to capture this iterative refinement and addresses challenges such as learning from long trajectories and reward attribution across turns. We present Kevin — K(ernel D)evin — the first model trained with multi-turn RL for CUDA kernel generation and optimization. In our evaluation, Kevin shows gains over its base model (QwQ-32B), improving correctness of generated kernels in pure CUDA and increasing mean speedup relative to a baseline execution mode. We compare behavior to other models and examine test-time scaling: scaling serial refinement appears more beneficial than parallel sampling, with more refinement turns often associated with further improvements. At the same time, the precise objective formulation and which parts of the RL recipe most critically drive gains remain underspecified, and we discuss open questions about reward design and evaluation that make the overall goals of kernel generation less clear-cut.

title: ORCaS: Unsupervised Depth Completion via Occluded Region Completion as Supervision
submission: We propose a method for inferring an egocentric dense depth map from an RGB image and a sparse point cloud. The crux of our method lies in modeling the 3D scene implicitly within the latent space and learning an inductive bias in an unsupervised manner through principles of Structure-from-Motion. To force the learning of this inductive bias, we optimize for an ill-posed objective during training: predicting latent features that are not observed in the input view but exist in the 3D scene. This is facilitated by rigid warping of latent features from the input view to a nearby or adjacent co-visible view. Empty regions in the latent space that correspond to occluded areas are completed by a Contextual eXtrapolation (ConteXt) mechanism based on features visible in the input. We term the approach Occluded Region Completion as Supervision (ORCaS). Preliminary experiments suggest benefits from this formulation, and further evaluation is left for future work.

title: Optimizing ID Consistency in Multimodal Large Models:  Facial Restoration via Alignment, Entanglement, and Disentanglement
submission: Multimodal editing large models enable a wide range of portrait edits, but maintaining facial identity (ID) consistency during realistic editing remains difficult. Existing approaches are limited by cross-source distribution biases and feature contamination that make joint preservation of identity and edited elements unreliable. We propose EditedID, an Alignment–Disentanglement–Entanglement framework for identity-specific facial restoration in multimodal editing. The framework centers on three components: an adaptive mixing strategy to align cross-source latents during diffusion, a hybrid solver intended to disentangle source-specific identity attributes from other details, and an attentional gating mechanism to selectively entangle visual elements. The design is deliberately training-free and plug-and-play to fit into existing pipelines. Empirical evaluation across a range of editing scenarios suggests EditedID can improve ID consistency in many cases, and we provide code and examples to facilitate further investigation.

submission: Understanding the interplay between intra-modality dependencies (an individual modality's contribution) and inter-modality dependencies (relationships between modalities and the target) is fundamental to multi-modal learning. However, the nature of and interaction between these dependencies in benchmarks remains poorly characterized. We present a large-scale empirical study attempting to quantify these dependencies across 23 visual question-answering benchmarks using multi-modal LLMs covering domains such as general and expert reasoning, OCR, and document understanding. Our findings indicate that reliance on vision, question (text), and their interaction varies significantly across and within benchmarks, and that some datasets intended to reduce text-only bias in fact amplify image-only signals. This pattern appears consistent across model sizes and types, with many models achieving high scores by exploiting single modalities rather than true interaction. We provide quantitative characterizations intended to inform benchmark design and evaluation, and discuss implications for future dataset construction and model assessment, though some details of the measurement choices are left for the reader to trace in the paper.

title: InterActHuman: Multi-Concept Human Animation with Layout-Aligned Audio Conditions
submission: End-to-end human animation with rich multi-modal conditions, e.g., text, image and audio has achieved remarkable advancements in recent years. However, most existing methods could only animate a single subject and inject conditions in a global manner, ignoring scenarios where multiple concepts could appear in the same video with rich human-human interactions and human-object interactions. Such a global assumption prevents precise and per-identity control of multiple concepts including humans and objects, therefore hinders applications. In this work, we discard the single-entity assumption and introduce a novel framework that enforces strong, region‑specific binding of conditions from modalities to each identity's spatiotemporal footprint. Given reference images of multiple concepts, our method could automatically infer layout information by leveraging a mask predictor to match appearance cues between the denoised video and each reference appearance. Furthermore, we inject local audio condition into its corresponding region to ensure layout-aligned modality matching in an iterative manner. This design enables the high-quality generation of human dialogue videos between two to three people or video customization from multiple reference images. Empirical results and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of our explicit layout control for multi-modal conditions compared to implicit counterparts and other existing methods.

title: TS-LIF: A Temporal Segment Spiking Neuron Network for Time Series Forecasting
submission: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer a biologically inspired approach for processing spatiotemporal data and are a promising direction for time series forecasting. Conventional neuron models like the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) can struggle to capture long-term dependencies and multi-scale temporal dynamics. To address these limitations, we introduce a Temporal Segment LIF (TS-LIF) idea that uses a dual-compartment notion: dendritic and somatic compartments are intended to specialize in different frequency components. We also propose to reduce intra-neuronal information loss via direct somatic current injection and to improve multi-scale extraction through dendritic spiking. The TS-LIF concept is motivated by stability considerations and distinct frequency responses across compartments. Preliminary experiments suggest the approach can improve forecasting accuracy and robustness under missing data. TS-LIF is presented as a biologically inspired direction for time-series forecasting that warrants further empirical and theoretical study.

title: OccProphet: Pushing the Efficiency Frontier of Camera-Only 4D Occupancy Forecasting with an Observer-Forecaster-Refiner Framework
submission: Predicting variations in complex traffic environments is crucial for the safety of autonomous driving. Recent advancements in occupancy forecasting have enabled forecasting future 3D occupied status in driving environments by observing historical 2D images. However, high computational demands make occupancy forecasting less efficient during training and inference stages, hindering its feasibility for deployment on edge agents. In this paper we propose a novel framework, i.e., OccProphet, to efficiently and effectively learn occupancy forecasting with significantly lower computational requirements while improving forecasting accuracy. OccProphet comprises three lightweight components: Observer, Forecaster, and Refiner. The Observer extracts spatio-temporal features from 3D multi-frame voxels using the proposed Efficient 4D Aggregation with Tripling-Attention Fusion, while the Forecaster and Refiner conditionally predict and refine future occupancy inferences. Experimental results on nuScenes, Lyft-Level5, and nuScenes-Occupancy datasets demonstrate that OccProphet is both training- and inference-friendly. OccProphet reduces 58%~78% of the computational cost with a 2.6× speedup compared with the state-of-the-art Cam4DOcc, and achieves 4%~18% relatively higher forecasting accuracy. Code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/JLChen-C/OccProphet.

title: Collapsed Language Models Promote Fairness
submission: To mitigate societal biases encoded in pretrained language models, many approaches have been proposed including prompting, data augmentation, and regularized fine-tuning. However, principled understanding of fairness and a consistently effective debiasing algorithm remain elusive. In this work we examine Neural Collapse — a phenomenon observed in last-layer representations and classifiers — focusing on fairness-related words and token representations. We observe that alignment patterns in collapsed representations correlate with certain debiasing behaviors, and this observation motivates a principled fine-tuning method intended to promote fairness while preserving performance on common NLU tasks. The method is simple to integrate with existing debiasing pipelines and is informed by the collapse structure in representations. We provide the code at https://github.com/Xujxyang/Fairness-NC-main and discuss implications for designing debiasing procedures, leaving detailed empirical evaluation for follow-up work.

title: AFlow: Automating Agentic Workflow Generation
submission: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for solving complex tasks by employing agentic workflows that follow detailed instructions and operational sequences. Constructing these workflows remains time-consuming, limiting scalability. We reformulate workflow optimization as a search over code-represented workflows, where LLM-invoking nodes are connected by edges. AFLOW is an automated framework that explores this space using a tree search strategy, iteratively refining workflows via code modification, tree-structured experience, and execution feedback. The framework is intended to reduce manual setup and to make workflow generation more automatic. We evaluate AFLOW on several benchmark datasets and observe that the approach can reliably discover effective workflows and enable smaller models to be more competitive on certain tasks while reducing inference cost. Code is available at https://github.com/FoundationAgents/AFlow.

title: On the Optimization Landscape of Low Rank Adaptation Methods for Large Language Models
submission: Low-rank adaptation methods such as LoRA add a trainable low-rank matrix to frozen pre-trained weights to reduce trainable parameters, while GaLore compresses the gradient matrix and has been reported to converge faster with lower memory. Despite empirical successes, their behavior lacks theoretical clarity. We analyze the optimization landscapes of LoRA, GaLore, and full-rank adaptation and argue that GaLore may exhibit fewer spurious local minima and a larger region satisfying a PL-like condition, which could explain improved convergence. Building on this analysis, we propose GaRare, which applies a gradient random projection to further reduce overhead. The paper focuses on conceptual landscape comparisons and presents sketch proofs for the claimed landscape differences, but does not present complete experimental verification or comprehensive empirical results here. As such, empirical support for GaRare's practical advantages is limited in this version and further experiments are needed to validate the theoretical claims.

title: FaceShot: Bring Any Character into Life
submission: In this paper, we present ***FaceShot***, a training-free portrait animation framework to bring any character into life from any driven video without fine-tuning or retraining. title: The Crucial Role of Samplers in Online Direct Preference Optimization
submission: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a stable and scalable method for language model alignment, yet the role of samplers in its optimization behavior is not fully understood. In this paper we analyze DPO's convergence under different sampling strategies in an exact-gradient setting and show that sampling choice materially affects convergence behavior. Motivated by this, we propose an online sampler tailored to DPO and adapt it for practical settings via posterior-informed sampling and logit mixing. We provide theoretical analysis characterizing improved convergence properties for our sampler and discuss how these insights inform algorithm design. We also describe practical adaptations and report experiments on standard alignment datasets; these experiments illustrate the benefits of sampler-aware DPO but do not attempt exhaustive comparisons to every prior method. Our analysis offers a path toward sampler-driven improvements in preference-based alignment.

title: ConFIG: Towards Conflict-free Training of Physics Informed Neural Networks
submission: The loss functions of many learning problems contain multiple additive terms that can disagree and yield conflicting update directions. For Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), loss terms on initial/boundary conditions and physics equations are particularly difficult. To improve learning this multi-objective task, we propose the ConFIG method, which provides conflict-free updates by ensuring a positive dot product between the final update and each loss-specific gradient. It also maintains consistent optimization rates for all loss terms and dynamically adjusts gradient magnitudes based on conflict levels, and leverages momentum by alternating the back-propagation of different loss terms. We provide a mathematical proof showing the convergence of the ConFIG method, and evaluate it across a range of PINN scenarios. ConFIG shows promising performance and runtime characteristics in our evaluations. Source code is available at https://tum-pbs.github.io/ConFIG

title: Task Adaptation from Skills: Information Geometry, Disentanglement, and New Objectives for Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning
submission: Unsupervised reinforcement learning (URL) aims to learn general skills for unseen downstream tasks. Mutual Information Skill Learning (MISL) maximizes the mutual information between states and skills but lacks sufficient theoretical analysis regarding how well its learned skills can initialize downstream policies. Our theoretical analysis shows that the diversity and separability of learned skills are critical to downstream task adaptation, and that MISL does not necessarily guarantee these properties. We propose a disentanglement metric LSEPIN and build an information-geometric connection between LSEPIN and downstream adaptation cost. Replacing KL divergence with the Wasserstein distance yields improved geometric properties, leading to a new objective WSEP. We argue WSEP is theoretically justified to aid task adaptation and, under mild assumptions, can provably discover all potentially optimal initial policies, offering a substantially stronger guarantee than MISL. We also introduce the practical algorithm PWSEP to realize these gains.

title: Ready-to-React: Online Reaction Policy for Two-Character Interaction Generation
submission: This paper addresses the task of generating two-character online interactions. Previously, two main settings existed for two-character interaction generation: (1) generating one's motions based on the counterpart's complete motion sequence, and (2) jointly generating two-character motions based on specific conditions. We argue that these settings fail to model the process of real-life two-character interactions, where humans react in real time and act as independent individuals. In contrast, we propose an online reaction policy, Ready-to-React, to generate the next character pose based on past observed motions. Each character has its own reaction policy as its brain, enabling them to interact like real humans in a streaming manner. Our policy is implemented by incorporating a diffusion head into an auto-regressive model, which can dynamically respond to the counterpart's motions while mitigating error accumulation. We conduct experiments on the boxing task; results indicate improvements over baselines in several settings, though further evaluation is needed. We plan to release code and data.

title: Lightning-Fast Image Inversion and Editing for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
submission:
Diffusion inversion is the problem of taking an image and a text prompt that describes it and finding a noise latent that would generate the exact same image. 
Most current deterministic inversion techniques operate by approximately solving an implicit equation and may converge slowly or yield poor reconstructed images.  We formulate the problem by finding the roots of an implicit equation and devlop a method to solve it efficiently. Our solution is based on Newton-Raphson (NR), a well-known technique in numerical analysis. We show that a vanilla application of NR is computationally infeasible while naively transforming it to a computationally tractable alternative tends to converge to out-of-distribution solutions, resulting in poor reconstruction and editing. We therefore derive an efficient guided formulation that fastly converges and provides high-quality reconstructions and editing. We showcase our method on real image editing with three popular open-sourced diffusion models: Stable Diffusion, SDXL-Turbo, and Flux with different deterministic schedulers. Our solution, **Guided Newton-Raphson Inversion**, inverts an image within 0.4 sec (on an A100 GPU) for few-step models (SDXL-Turbo and Flux.1),
opening the door for interactive image editing. We further show improved results in image interpolation and generation of rare objects.

title: Local Patterns Generalize Better for Novel Anomalies
submission: We propose a framework that identifies local patterns which generalize to novel samples and models their dynamics. The extraction of spatial local patterns is achieved via a two-stage process combining image-text alignment and cross-modality attention. Generalizable representations focus on semantically relevant components that can be recombined to capture novel anomalies, reducing unnecessary visual variance. To inject temporal cues into local patterns, we propose a State Machine Module (SMM) that uses earlier high-resolution textual tokens to guide captioning for later low-resolution observations. Temporal motion estimation complements spatial local patterns to detect anomalies characterized by novel spatial distributions or distinctive dynamics. Extensive experiments on popular benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/AllenYLJiang/Local-Patterns-Generalize-Better/.

title: Zero-shot Imputation with Foundation Inference Models for Dynamical Systems
submission: Dynamical systems governed by ordinary differential equations (ODEs) serve as models for a vast number of natural and social phenomena, and missing data in such time series is a pervasive challenge in science and engineering. In this work, we revisit the classical problem of imputing missing time series data whose underlying dynamics are assumed to be determined by ODEs. We propose a supervised framework for zero-shot time series imputation through parametric functions satisfying some (hidden) ODEs. Our approach has two components. First, we define a broad probability distribution over the space of ODE solutions, observation times and noise mechanisms, and generate a large synthetic dataset of hidden ODE solutions along with noisy sparse observations. Second, an offline-trained neural recognition model maps generated time series onto initial conditions and time derivatives of the hidden ODE solutions; we then integrate these to impute missing data. Empirically, a single pretrained recognition model can perform zero-shot imputation across dozens of distinct time series and across diverse high-dimensional settings such as human motion, air quality, traffic, electricity studies and Navier–Stokes simulations — often without any fine-tuning. Our pretrained model, repository and tutorials are available online.

title: Add-it: Training-Free Object Insertion in Images With Pretrained Diffusion Models
submission: Adding object into images based on text instructions is a challenging task in semantic image editing it requires balancing preserving the original scene and integrating the new object in a fitting location. Despite extensive efforts, existing models often struggle, particularly finding a natural location for adding an object in complex scenes. We introduce Add-it, a training-free approach that extends diffusion models' attention mechanisms to incorporate information from three sources: the scene image, the text prompt and the generated image itself. Our weighted extended-attention mechanism maintains structural consistency and fine details while ensuring natural object placement, it uses attention weights that combine multiple cues and iteratively refines placement. Without task-specific fine-tuning, Add-it achieves state-of-the-art results on both real and generated image insertion benchmarks, including our newly constructed "Additing Affordance Benchmark" for evaluating object placement plausibility; human evaluations show Add-it is preferred in over 80% of cases and it also demonstrates improvements in various automated metrics.

title: Do Vision & Language Decoders use Images and Text equally? How Self-consistent are their Explanations?
submission: Vision and language model (VLM) decoders are currently strong architectures for multimodal tasks and can produce natural language explanations in post-hoc or chain-of-thought (CoT) settings. In this work we study whether VLM decoders rely on vision and text inputs differently when generating answers versus explanations, and how self-consistent their outputs are. To that end we extend a set of unimodal tests and consistency measures to the multimodal decoder setting and run evaluations across several recent models. Our experiments indicate that many tested VLMs show lower self-consistency than large language models and that text signals often dominate image signals in the examined tasks. There are also differences between explanation generation and answer generation, and between CoT and post-hoc explanations, but effect sizes are mixed and dataset-dependent. Finally, we provide benchmarking on the VALSE suite for decoder models and release code to facilitate further study.

title: 6DGS: Enhanced Direction-Aware Gaussian Splatting for Volumetric Rendering
submission: Novel view synthesis has advanced significantly with the development of neural radiance fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS). In this work we revisit 6D Gaussians and introduce 6D Gaussian Splatting (6DGS), which enhances color and opacity representations and leverages the additional directional information in the 6D space for optimized Gaussian control. Our approach is fully compatible with the 3DGS framework and is designed to improve real-time radiance field rendering by modeling view-dependent effects and fine details. We change the Gaussian representation and control scheme, and describe how these adjustments integrate with existing splatting pipelines. Experiments compare 6DGS, 3DGS and N-DG, showing substantial improvements: up to a 15.73 dB improvement in PSNR with a reduction of 66.5% Gaussian points compared to 3DGS. The project page is: https://gaozhongpai.github.io/6dgs/.

title: ESE: Espresso Sentence Embeddings
submission: High-quality sentence embeddings are fundamental in many NLP tasks such as semantic textual similarity and retrieval-augmented generation. We propose Espresso Sentence Embeddings (ESE), a sentence embedding model that uses two complementary learning processes. The first, a learn-to-express process, encourages salient representations to appear in shallower layers. The second, a learn-to-compress process, compacts essential features into the initial embedding dimensions via Principal Component Analysis. Together these components let ESE scale model depth and embedding size. Extensive experiments on STS and RAG are reported, suggesting ESE can produce effective sentence embeddings with reduced depth and smaller embedding size, improving inference efficiency. The code is available at https://github.com/SeanLee97/AnglE/blob/main/README_ESE.md.

title: Safety Layers in Aligned Large Language Models: The Key to LLM Security
submission: Aligned LLMs are secure, capable of recognizing and refusing to answer malicious questions. However, the role of internal parameters in maintaining such security is not well understood yet, further these models can be vulnerable to security degradation when subjected to fine-tuning attacks. To address these challenges, our work uncovers the mechanism behind security in aligned LLMs at the parameter level, identifying a small set of contiguous layers in the middle of the model that are crucial for distinguishing malicious queries from normal ones, referred to as "safety layers". We first confirm the existence of these safety layers by analyzing variations in input vectors within the model's internal layers. Additionally, we leverage the over-rejection phenomenon and parameters scaling analysis to precisely locate the safety layers. Building on these findings, we propose a novel fine-tuning approach, Safely Partial-Parameter Fine-Tuning (SPPFT), that fixes the gradient of the safety layers during fine-tuning to address the security degradation. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly preserve LLM security while maintaining performance and reducing computational resources compared to full fine-tuning.

title: Jailbreak Antidote: Runtime Safety-Utility Balance via Sparse Representation Adjustment in Large Language Models
submission: As large language models (LLMs) become integral to various applications, ensuring both their safety and utility is paramount. Jailbreak attacks manipulate models into generating harmful content, and defenses often add computational overhead or lack runtime flexibility. We introduce Jailbreak Antidote, a method that enables real-time adjustment of LLM safety preferences by manipulating a sparse subset of internal states during inference. By shifting hidden representations along a safety direction with varying strengths, the method aims to control the safety-utility balance without additional token overhead or inference delays. Our analysis suggests safety-related information is sparsely distributed, and that adjusting approximately 5% of the internal state can be effective. We evaluate nine LLMs against ten jailbreak methods and compare with existing defenses. By directly manipulating internal states during reasoning, Jailbreak Antidote proposes a lightweight, scalable mechanism intended to enhance safety while preserving utility, though practical trade-offs and deployment details require further exploration.

title: A General Framework for Off-Policy Learning with Partially-Observed Reward
submission: Off-policy learning (OPL) in contextual bandits aims to learn a decision-making policy that maximizes the target rewards by using only historical interaction data collected under previously developed policies. Unfortunately, when rewards are only partially observed, the effectiveness of OPL degrades severely. Well-known examples of such partial rewards include explicit ratings in content recommendations, conversion signals on e-commerce platforms that are partial due to delay, and the issue of censoring in medical problems. One possible solution to deal with such partial rewards is to use secondary rewards, such as dwelling time, clicks, and medical indicators, which are more densely observed. However, relying solely on such secondary rewards can also lead to poor policy learning since they may not align with the target reward. Thus, this work studies a new and general problem of OPL where the goal is to learn a policy that maximizes the expected target reward by leveraging densely observed secondary rewards as supplemental data. We then propose a new method called Hybrid Policy Optimization for Partially-Observed Reward (HyPeR), which effectively uses the secondary rewards in addition to the partially observed target reward to achieve effective OPL despite the challenging scenario. We also discuss a case where we aim to optimize not only the expected target reward but also the expected secondary rewards to some extent; counter-intuitively, we will show that leveraging the two objectives is in fact advantageous also for the optimization of only the target reward. Along with statistical analysis of our proposed methods, empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world data show that HyPeR outperforms existing methods in various scenarios.

title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Transformer
submission: Transformers are the cornerstone of modern deep learning and traditionally rely on multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) to mix channel information. Much prior work studies how MLPs and attention interact, and how activation functions and basis choices affect representational capacity. In this paper, we introduce the Kolmogorov–Arnold Transformer (KAT), which replaces MLP layers with Kolmogorov–Arnold Network (KAN) layers to enhance expressiveness and performance. Integrating KANs at scale raises challenges: the standard B-spline base function is not ideal for parallel GPU computation; KANs can be parameter- and computation-heavy because they naively require unique functions per input-output pair; and learnable activations complicate weight initialization. To address these, we propose using rational basis functions for better GPU compatibility, sharing activation weights across groups to reduce cost, and variance-preserving initialization to maintain activation statistics. With these designs KAT scales effectively. We demonstrate advantages of KAT across image recognition, object detection, and segmentation, and discuss how the KAN perspective connects to known transformer behaviors.

title: AutomaTikZ: Text-Guided Synthesis of Scientific Vector Graphics with TikZ
submission: Generating bitmap graphics from text has gained considerable attention, yet for scientific figures, vector graphics are often preferred. Given that vector graphics are typically encoded using low-level graphics primitives, generating them directly is difficult. We propose the use of TikZ, a well-known abstract graphics language that can be compiled to vector graphics, as an intermediate representation of scientific figures. TikZ offers human-oriented, high-level commands, thereby facilitating conditional language modeling with any large language model. To this end, we introduce DaTikZ the first large-scale TikZ dataset, consisting of 120k TikZ drawings aligned with captions. We fine-tune LLaMA on DaTikZ, as well as our new model CLiMA, which augments LLaMA with multimodal CLIP embeddings. In both human and automatic evaluation, CLiMA and LLaMA outperform commercial systems in terms of similarity to human-created figures. We make our framework, AutomaTikZ, along with model weights and datasets, publicly available.

title: RocketEval: Efficient automated LLM evaluation via grading checklist
submission: Evaluating large language models (LLMs) across diverse scenarios is crucial for aligning them with human preferences, yet human evaluation is costly. Using a lightweight LLM as a judge offers a practical alternative but can suffer from uncertainty and positional bias compared to more powerful judges. We propose RocketEval, an automated evaluation pipeline that reframes evaluation as a multi-faceted Q&A using an instance-specific checklist. RocketEval constructs checklists, has lightweight LLMs grade those items, and then reweights checklist components to better align with available supervised annotations. This checklist grading approach aims to reduce uncertainty and positional effects without relying on expensive judgement models. We validate RocketEval on commonly used automated evaluation benchmarks and find it produces stable and interpretable scores across diverse prompts. In large-scale settings, RocketEval substantially reduces evaluation cost and operational complexity while remaining straightforward to reproduce using modest judge models.

title: Multimodal Lego: Model Merging and Fine-Tuning Across Topologies and Modalities in Biomedicine
submission: Learning holistic computational representations in physical, chemical or biological systems requires processing information from different distributions and modalities within the same model. The demand for multimodal models has sharply risen for modalities beyond vision and language, such as sequences, graphs, time series, or tabular data. While many fusion and alignment approaches exist, they often require end-to-end training, scale poorly with modalities, or are topology-specific. We present Multimodal Lego (MM-Lego), a general-purpose fusion framework designed to turn any set of encoders into a multimodal model with no or minimal fine-tuning. MM-Lego introduces a wrapper for unimodal encoders that enforces shape consistency between modality representations and harmonises these representations by learning features in the frequency domain to enable model merging with reduced signal interference. We illustrate how MM-Lego can be applied as a model-merging method, can operate with diverse unimodal encoders, and with light tuning can improve performance on several biomedical datasets, suggesting broad applicability for multimodal biomedical tasks.

title: LeFusion: Controllable Pathology Synthesis via Lesion-Focused Diffusion Models
submission: Patient data from real-world clinical practice often suffers from data scarcity and long-tail imbalances, leading to biased outcomes or algorithmic unfairness. This study addresses these challenges by generating lesion-containing image-segmentation pairs from lesion-free images. Previous efforts in medical imaging synthesis have struggled with separating lesion information from background, resulting in low-quality backgrounds and limited control over the synthetic output. Inspired by diffusion-based image inpainting, we propose LeFusion, a lesion-focused diffusion model. By redesigning the diffusion learning objectives to focus on lesion areas, we simplify the learning process and improve control over the output while preserving high-fidelity backgrounds by integrating forward-diffused background contexts into the reverse diffusion process. Additionally, we tackle two major challenges in lesion texture synthesis: 1) multi-peak and 2) multi-class lesions. We introduce two effective strategies: histogram-based texture control and multi-channel decomposition, enabling the controlled generation of high-quality lesions in difficult scenarios. Furthermore, we incorporate lesion mask diffusion, allowing control over lesion size, location, and boundary, thus increasing lesion diversity. Validated on 3D cardiac lesion MRI and lung nodule CT datasets, LeFusion-generated data significantly improves the performance of state-of-the-art segmentation models, including nnUNet and SwinUNETR.

title: Open-World Reinforcement Learning over Long Short-Term Imagination
submission: Training visual reinforcement learning agents in a high-dimensional open world presents significant challenges. While various model-based methods have improved sample efficiency by learning interactive world models, these agents tend to be “short-sighted”, as they are typically trained on short snippets of imagined experiences. We argue that the primary challenge in open-world decision-making is improving the exploration efficiency across a vast state space, especially for tasks that demand consideration of long-horizon payoffs. In this paper, we present LS-Imagine, which extends the imagination horizon within a limited number of state transition steps, enabling the agent to explore behaviors that potentially lead to promising long-term feedback. The foundation of our approach is to build a $\textit{long short-term world model}$. To achieve this, we simulate goal-conditioned jumpy state transitions and compute corresponding affordance maps by zooming in on specific areas within single images. This facilitates the integration of direct long-term values into behavior learning. Our method demonstrates significant improvements over state-of-the-art techniques in MineDojo.

title: Matérn Kernels for Tunable Implicit Surface Reconstruction
submission: Kernel methods have long provided principled tools for function approximation and regularization, and recently they have been re-examined in the context of 3D reconstruction where their theoretical grounding and computational properties are attractive. In this work we propose the family of Matérn kernels for implicit surface reconstruction, building upon recent success of kernel methods for 3D reconstruction of oriented point clouds. From both theoretical and practical perspectives we show Matérn kernels have appealing properties which make them particularly well suited for surface reconstruction—outperforming methods based on the arc-cosine kernel while being easier to implement, faster to compute, and scalable. Being stationary, Matérn kernels allow tunable surface reconstruction similarly to how Fourier feature mappings help coordinate-based MLPs overcome spectral bias. title: Scalable Diffusion for Materials Generation
submission: Generative models trained on internet-scale data have advanced text, image, and video synthesis, and it is natural to ask whether they can help generate novel materials. Models with explicit structures (for example graphs) have traditionally been used to model atoms and bonds in crystals, but scaling such structured generators to large, complex systems is challenging. We tackle scalability by developing a unified crystal representation, UniMat, that can represent arbitrary crystal structures, and then train a diffusion probabilistic model on these representations. Empirically, UniMat can produce high-fidelity crystal structures from larger chemical systems and compares favorably to prior graph-based approaches on several generative modeling metrics. title: Understanding Matrix Function Normalizations in Covariance Pooling through the Lens of Riemannian Geometry
submission: Global Covariance Pooling (GCP) leverages second-order statistics of high-level representations and often normalizes covariance matrices via matrix logarithm or power prior to a Euclidean classifier. Covariance matrices, however, reside on the Symmetric Positive Definite (SPD) Riemannian manifold, and the literature lacks a fully satisfying account of why Euclidean classifiers work after matrix power normalization. In this paper we provide a unified perspective based on Riemannian geometry and interpret matrix logarithm and power from two viewpoints: tangent classifiers (Euclidean classifiers on the tangent space) and Riemannian classifiers. We outline theoretical connections that suggest matrix functions implicitly respect certain Riemannian classifiers. While we sketch these interpretations and their implications for representation learning on SPD manifolds, we do not provide detailed algorithmic procedures or comprehensive experimental results in this version; the discussion is intended as a conceptual framework to motivate future formal analysis and empirical validation. Code resources are referenced for subsequent study.

title: Backtracking Improves Generation Safety
submission: Text generation has a fundamental limitation almost by definition: there is no taking back tokens that have been generated, even when they are clearly problematic. In the context of language model safety, when a partial unsafe generation is produced, language models by their nature tend to happily keep on generating similarly unsafe additional text. This is in fact how safety alignment of frontier models gets circumvented in the wild, despite great efforts in improving their safety. Deviating from the paradigm of approaching safety alignment as prevention (decreasing the probability of harmful responses), we propose backtracking, a technique that allows language models to "undo" and recover from their own unsafe generation through the introduction of a special [RESET] token. Our method can be incorporated into either SFT or DPO training to optimize helpfulness and harmlessness. We report that models trained with backtracking show safety benefits on constrained synthetic tests; however, gains are inconsistent across broader benchmarks and do not uniformly match the intuitions behind the method. The approach nonetheless provides an avenue for recovery-based safety interventions and resilience to some adversarial patterns.

title: Consistency-guided Prompt Learning for Vision-Language Models
submission: We propose Consistency-guided Prompt learning (CoPrompt), a new fine-tuning method for vision-language models. In recent years, foundation models trained on massive image-text corpora have become ubiquitous, and a large body of work has explored prompt tuning, adapter methods, and hybrid approaches to adapt these models to downstream tasks. Few-shot adaptation is particularly challenging: with very limited labeled examples models often overfit, and various regularization and prompt design strategies have been proposed to mitigate this. CoPrompt builds on this prior work by enforcing a consistency constraint between the predictions of a trainable model and the pre-trained model to prevent overfitting. In addition, we enforce consistency across two perturbed inputs and combine prompting with adapters to increase flexibility in both input and output spaces. Enforcing consistency on perturbed inputs further regularizes the model and aims to improve generalization in few-shot settings. Experiments on several evaluation suites show that CoPrompt compares favorably to existing approaches, and ablation studies highlight the role of each component. Code is available at https://github.com/ShuvenduRoy/CoPrompt.

title: Linear Spherical Sliced Optimal Transport: A Fast Metric for Comparing Spherical Data
submission: Efficient comparison of spherical probability distributions is important in computer vision, geosciences, and medicine. We demonstrate the idea in GNN architecture design with a KBG built from extensive records and validate its utility for guiding design choices.

title: Mufu:  Multilingual Fused Learning for Low-Resource Translation with LLM
submission: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) are great translators, but this is largely limited to high-resource languages. For many LLMs, translating in and out of low-resource languages remains a challenging task. To maximize data efficiency in this low-resource setting, we introduce Mufu, which includes a selection of automatically generated multilingual candidates and an instruction to correct inaccurate translations in the prompt. Mufu prompts turn a translation task into a postediting one, and seek to harness the LLM’s reasoning capability with auxiliary translation candidates, from which the model is required to assess the input quality, align the semantics cross-lingually, copy from relevant inputs and override instances that are incorrect. We then distill these models to reduce inference cost, while maintaining on average 3.1 chrF improvement over finetune-only baseline in low-resource translations.

title: Strategic Classification With Externalities
submission: We propose a new variant of the strategic classification problem: a principal reveals a classifier, and n agents report their (possibly manipulated) features to be classified. Motivated by real-world applications, our model allows one agent's manipulation to affect another; it explicitly captures inter-agent externalities. Principal-agent interactions are modeled as a Stackelberg game, with the resulting agent manipulation dynamics captured as a simultaneous game. Under certain assumptions we outline conditions under which a pure Nash equilibrium of this agent manipulation game is unique and describe an algorithmic approach for computing it; however, we do not provide full constructive proofs or empirical validation of the solver here. Leveraging this equilibrium characterization, we sketch PAC-style learning guarantees suggesting that classifiers minimizing expected loss can be learned even when a random subset of agents manipulate features toward an equilibrium. We do not include direct comparisons to prior baselines or empirical benchmarks in this exposition, and leave extensive empirical evaluation to future work.

title: HiSplat: Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting for Generalizable Sparse-View Reconstruction
submission: Reconstructing 3D scenes from multiple viewpoints is a central task in stereo vision. Recent work on generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting predicts per-pixel Gaussian parameters feed-forward for unseen scenes, avoiding per-scene optimization. However, single-scale 3D Gaussians often lack representation of both large-scale structure and texture, causing mislocation and artifacts. We propose HiSplat, a hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that constructs hierarchical 3D Gaussians in a coarse-to-fine manner: coarse-grained Gaussians capture large-scale structure while fine-grained Gaussians enhance texture. To promote inter-scale interaction, we introduce an Error Aware Module for Gaussian compensation and a Modulating Fusion Module for Gaussian repair, enabling joint optimization of hierarchical representations. HiSplat enables novel view synthesis using only a single-view reference image. We include ablations and analysis of different-scale Gaussians to illustrate the mechanism behind the approach.

title: Impact of Computation in Integral Reinforcement Learning for Continuous-Time Control
submission: Integral reinforcement learning (IntRL) relies on accurately computing integrals of the utility during policy evaluation, typically via quadrature over discrete-time state samples. We study how the choice of quadrature and computational method affects downstream control performance. By drawing an analogy between IntRL policy iteration and Newton’s method for the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation, we argue that computational error in policy evaluation appears as an additional error term in each iteration, and that its magnitude controls the iteration behavior. We further discuss that when the utility lies in an RKHS, Bayesian quadrature with the RKHS kernel can be used as a principled alternative to simple rules. Based on this perspective we outline expected local convergence behavior for some common quadratures and present limited empirical validation on two canonical control tasks. The paper focuses on conceptual connections between computation and control rather than exhaustive algorithmic prescriptions.

title: Heavy-Tailed Diffusion with Denoising Levy Probabilistic Models
submission: Investigating noise distributions beyond Gaussian in diffusion generative models remains an open challenge. The Gaussian case has been a large success experimentally and theoretically, admitting a unified stochastic differential equation (SDE) framework, encompassing score-based and denoising formulations. Recent studies have investigated the potential of heavy-tailed noise distributions to mitigate mode collapse and to better handle datasets with class imbalance, heavy tails, or prominent outliers. Very recently, Yoon et al. (NeurIPS 2023) presented the L\'evy-Ito model (LIM), directly extending the SDE-based framework to a class of heavy-tailed SDEs where the injected noise followed an alpha-stable distribution. Despite this progress, many aspects of non-Gaussian diffusion remain underexplored, including practical algorithmic choices, implementation accessibility, and applicability across domains. In this work, we take a step back from the SDE formulation and extend the denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) by replacing Gaussian noise with alpha-stable noise. Using elementary proof techniques, we show the resulting denoising L\'evy probabilistic model (DLPM) can be implemented with minimal changes to standard DDPM pipelines, while highlighting conceptual distinctions from LIM regarding training and backward processes.

title: SSOLE: Rethinking Orthogonal Low-rank Embedding for Self-Supervised Learning
submission: Self-supervised learning (SSL) seeks meaningful representations from unlabeled data. Orthogonal Low-rank Embedding (OLE) encourages intra-class low-rank structure and inter-class high-rank separation, which is attractive for multi-view learning, but directly applying OLE in SSL is challenging: there are effectively infinite "classes" in SSL and low-rank constraints can conflate positively and negatively correlated features. We introduce SSOLE (Self-Supervised Orthogonal Low-rank Embedding), which adapts OLE principles to SSL by decoupling low-rank and high-rank enforcement and by applying low-rank constraints to feature deviations from their mean so as to respect sign information in cosine similarities. We provide theoretical rationale for these modifications and describe an efficient implementation that does not require large batches, memory banks, or dual encoders. Experiments across standard SSL benchmarks are reported to support the approach, but we leave detailed metric-level comparisons and ablations for the main text and code.

title: Laplace Sample Information:  Data Informativeness Through a Bayesian Lens
submission: Estimating the informativeness of individual samples is useful for guiding sample selection in deep learning. We propose Laplace Sample Information (LSI), an information-theoretic measure grounded in a Bayesian Laplace approximation to the weight posterior that uses KL divergence to quantify the change in the parameter distribution induced by a sample. We argue LSI is broadly applicable across architectures and learning settings, and we present experiments on image and text data in supervised and unsupervised settings. Empirical results indicate LSI can help rank typical versus atypical examples and detect some mislabeled samples; however, evaluations are limited in scope and some findings are mixed with respect to class-wise informativeness and transfer to large-model training. We also describe efficient probe-based approximations for computing LSI, and discuss avenues for scaling and more comprehensive evaluation.

title: SaRA: High-Efficient Diffusion Model Fine-tuning with Progressive Sparse Low-Rank Adaptation
submission: The development of diffusion models has led to significant progress in image and video generation tasks, with pre-trained models like the Stable Diffusion series playing a crucial role. However, adapting pre-trained diffusion models to new downstream tasks remains challenging. Inspired by pruning that lightens models by removing unimportant parameters, we propose a fine-tuning approach that reutilizes parameters that appear ineffective after pre-training. We first investigate parameter importance in pre-trained diffusion models and observe that parameters with the smallest absolute values are often inactive during generation. Based on this, we introduce SaRA, which optimizes a sparse weight matrix to absorb task-specific knowledge by reassigning those parameters. To reduce overfitting we employ a low-rank sparse training scheme and a progressive parameter adjustment strategy, and we also propose an unstructured backpropagation variant to lower memory costs during fine-tuning. Empirically, SaRA improves downstream generative behavior while better preserving generalization compared to standard fine-tuning baselines.

submission: We present VEDIT, a latent prediction architecture for procedural video representation learning. submission: Large language models (LLMs) have advanced many NLP tasks, including question answering (QA). title: Sequential Stochastic Combinatorial Optimization Using Hierarchal Reinforcement Learning
submission:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising tool for combinatorial optimization (CO) problems due to its ability to learn fast, effective, and generalizable solutions. 
Nonetheless, existing works mostly focus on one-shot deterministic CO, while sequential stochastic CO (SSCO) has rarely been studied despite its broad applications such as adaptive influence maximization (IM) and infectious disease intervention. 
In this paper, we study the SSCO problem where we first decide the budget (e.g., number of seed nodes in adaptive IM) allocation for all time steps, and then select a set of nodes for each time step. The few existing studies on SSCO simplify the problems by assuming a uniformly distributed budget allocation over the time horizon, yielding suboptimal solutions. We propose a generic hierarchical RL (HRL) framework called wake-sleep option (WS-option), a two-layer option-based framework that simultaneously decides adaptive budget allocation on the higher layer and node selection on the lower layer. 
WS-option starts with a coherent formulation of the two-layer Markov decision processes (MDPs), capturing the interdependencies between the two layers of decisions. Building on this, WS-option employs several innovative designs to balance the model's training stability and computational efficiency, preventing the vicious cyclic interference issue between the two layers. Empirical results show that WS-option exhibits significantly improved effectiveness and generalizability compared to traditional methods. Moreover, the learned model can be generalized to larger graphs, which significantly reduces the overhead of computational resources.

title: WavTokenizer: an Efficient Acoustic Discrete Codec Tokenizer for Audio Language Modeling
submission: We introduce WavTokenizer, an acoustic discrete codec tokenizer for audio language modeling that emphasizes strong compression and compact semantic representations. By compressing quantizer layers and the temporal dimension, a one-second 24 kHz clip can be represented with a single quantizer using on the order of tens of tokens (e.g., 40 or 75 tokens). The design uses a broader VQ space, extended contextual windows, enhanced attention blocks, a multi-scale discriminator, and an inverse Fourier structure. We conducted reconstruction experiments across speech, audio, and music and report favorable UTMOS and objective scores. We also probe semantic content, VQ utilization, and adaptability to generative models. Ablation studies suggest each module contributes to overall performance, though some effects are modest and task-dependent. Implementation details and code are available.

title: Neural Approximate Mirror Maps for Constrained Diffusion Models
submission: Diffusion models create visually convincing images but often struggle to satisfy subtle constraints present in training data, such as physics-based, geometric, or semantic constraints. When training data all satisfy a constraint, enforcing it in the generative model yields more reliable synthetic data and helps solve constrained inverse problems. Recent mirror diffusion models (MDMs) rely on analytical mirror maps, which are available mainly for convex constraints. We propose neural approximate mirror maps (NAMMs) for general, possibly non-convex constraints. Our approach requires only a differentiable distance function from the constraint set, and learns an approximate mirror map that transforms data into an unconstrained space, together with an approximate inverse that maps samples back to the constraint set. A generative model can then be trained in the learned mirror space and restored by the inverse map. We validate NAMMs on a variety of constraints and observe improved constraint satisfaction in practice, suggesting wider applicability for constrained inverse problems.

title: Recovery of Causal Graph Involving Latent Variables via Homologous Surrogates
submission: Causal discovery with latent variables is important but challenging. Existing methods often rely on the pure-child assumption for latent identification; here we introduce the concept of a homologous surrogate to relax that requirement. A homologous surrogate differs from a pure child by allowing more flexible parent sets. We state two assumptions involving homologous surrogates and provide theoretical claims under each: under a weaker assumption we claim one can determine ancestors (a partial recovery), while under a stronger assumption we claim full recovery of parents. Building on these claims, we derive an algorithm intended to exploit homologous surrogates to recover causal structure. However, the algorithm's stated guarantees are not uniform: in some cases it recovers only ancestor relations, while in others it purports exact parent recovery, leaving the exact operational conditions somewhat ambiguous. We include experimental illustrations to indicate where each outcome occurs and provide code at the project repository.

title: How do Language Models Bind Entities in Context?
submission: Language models (LMs) can recall facts mentioned in context, as shown by their performance on reading comprehension tasks. title: ST-GCond: Self-supervised and Transferable Graph Dataset Condensation
submission: Graph dataset condensation aims to reduce large graph datasets to compact, informative ones that preserve downstream performance. Existing methods, however, often fail to generalize when the downstream task or dataset differs from the original. To address cross-task and cross-dataset transferability, we present ST-GCond: Self-supervised and Transferable Graph dataset Condensation. For cross-task transferability, we introduce a task-disentangled meta-optimization strategy that adaptively updates the condensed graph according to task relevance, encouraging preservation of task-relevant information. For cross-dataset transferability, we employ a multi-teacher self-supervised optimization to inject universal structural and semantic knowledge into the condensed graph. We further incorporate a mutual-information-guided joint condensation objective to mitigate conflicts and stabilize training. Experiments on node- and graph-level datasets show that ST-GCond consistently outperforms prior condensation methods in cross-task and cross-dataset scenarios, yielding improvements in a range of transfer settings and achieving state-of-the-art results on most benchmarks we evaluate.

title: Nonlinear multiregion neural dynamics with parametric impulse response communication channels
submission: Cognition arises from coordinated interactions of brain regions with distinct computational roles. Despite progress in extracting dynamics from population activity in individual areas, understanding how multiple areas jointly support distributed computation remains challenging. We propose a multi-region neural dynamics model composed of two building blocks: (i) within-region (potentially driven) nonlinear dynamics and (ii) communication channels between regions parameterized by their impulse response. These choices make it possible to learn nonlinear neural population dynamics while leveraging ideas from linear systems theory to study inter-regional information flow. We develop a state-noise-inversion-free variational filtering and learning algorithm for the model and show, through neuroscientifically inspired numerical experiments, how the model can reveal interpretable characterizations of local computations and the flow of information between populations. We also apply the approach to simultaneous population recordings from areas V1 and V2, providing preliminary validation and insights that merit further study rather than definitive conclusions.

title: PT-T2I/V: An Efficient Proxy-Tokenized Diffusion Transformer for Text-to-Image/Video-Task
submission: The global self-attention mechanism in diffusion transformers involves redundant computation due to the sparse and redundant nature of visual information, and the attention map of tokens within a spatial window shows significant similarity. To address this redundancy, we propose the Proxy-Tokenized Diffusion Transformer (PT-DiT), which employs sparse representative token attention (where the number of representative tokens is much smaller than the total number of tokens) to efficiently model global visual information. Specifically, within each transformer block, we compute an averaging token from each spatial-temporal window to serve as a proxy token for that region. The global semantics are captured through the self-attention of these proxy tokens and then injected into all latent tokens via cross-attention. Simultaneously, we introduce window and shift window attention to address the limitations in detail modeling caused by the sparse attention mechanism. Building on the well-designed PT-DiT, we further develop the PT-T2I/V family, which includes a variety of models for T2I, T2V, and T2MV tasks. Experimental results show that PT-DiT achieves competitive performance while reducing computational complexity in image and video generation tasks (e.g., a reduction 59\% compared to DiT and a reduction 34\% compared to PixArt-$\alpha$). The visual exhibition of and code are available at https://360cvgroup.github.io/Qihoo-T2X/.

title: Personalized Visual Instruction Tuning
submission: Recent advancements in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated significant progress; however, these models exhibit a notable limitation, which we refer to as "face blindness." Specifically, they can engage in general conversations but fail to conduct personalized dialogues targeting at specific individuals. This deficiency hinders the application of MLLMs in personalized settings, such as tailored visual assistants on mobile devices, or domestic robots that need to recognize members of the family. In this paper, we introduce Personalized Visual Instruction Tuning (PVIT), a novel data curation and training framework designed to enable MLLMs to identify target individuals within an image and engage in personalized and coherent dialogues. Our approach involves the development of a sophisticated pipeline that autonomously generates training data containing personalized conversations. This pipeline leverages the capabilities of various visual experts, image generation models, and (multi-modal) large language models. To evaluate the personalized potential of MLLMs, we present a benchmark called P-Bench, which encompasses various question types with different levels of difficulty. The experiments demonstrate a substantial personalized performance enhancement after fine-tuning with our curated dataset.

title: kNN Attention Demystified: A Theoretical Exploration for Scalable Transformers
submission: Transformers face challenges with long sequences due to quadratic self-attention complexity. To mitigate this, k-Nearest-Neighbor (kNN) attention permits each token to attend only to its k closest tokens, which has been used empirically to improve efficiency. Despite empirical success, exact approximation guarantees for kNN attention have not been fully analyzed. Here we establish a theoretical framework for kNN attention, reformulating self-attention as expectations over softmax distributions and leveraging lazy Gumbel sampling with kNN indices for efficient approximation. Building on this view, we propose sub-quadratic algorithms that approximate self-attention gradients by leveraging efficient sampling techniques, including Markov Chain-based estimation. We describe algorithmic details and present empirical experiments to illustrate behavior and costs. While the framework clarifies approximation mechanisms and suggests possible practical gains, we do not provide head-to-head baseline comparisons here and present the empirical results as preliminary illustrations of feasibility rather than definitive performance claims.

title: Contextual Self-paced Learning for Weakly Supervised Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding
submission: We study Weakly Supervised Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding (WSTVG), a multimodal task that aims to localize subjects in space and time from textual queries without bounding box supervision. Motivated by advances in multimodal foundation models, we explore adapting off-the-shelf object detectors to WSTVG but note several limitations when applied naively. To address these, we propose CoSPaL (Contextual Self-Paced Learning), which integrates three components: Tubelet Phrase Grounding (TPG) for spatio-temporal prediction via tubelets; Contextual Referral Grounding (CRG) to extract contextual cues for refining object identification over time; and Self-Paced Scene Understanding (SPS), a curriculum that transitions from coarse to fine-grained examples. The paper describes the design and training of these modules. While the approach is conceptually motivated for complex queries and difficult scenarios, concrete experimental validation and quantitative comparisons are not provided here, and further work is needed to establish empirical gains.

title: Debiasing Mini-Batch Quadratics for Applications in Deep Learning
submission: Quadratic approximations form a fundamental building block of many machine learning methods. For example, second-order optimizers aim to find a Newton step into the minimum of a local quadratic proxy to the objective; similarly, the second-order approximation of a network's loss is used to quantify output uncertainty via the Laplace approximation. When computations on the entire training set are intractable—as is typical in deep learning—relevant quantities are computed on mini-batches. Unfortunately, this distorts and biases the shape of the associated stochastic quadratic approximations in an intricate way with detrimental effects on applications. The literature on Hessian approximations, Gauss-Newton and generalized Gauss-Newton, block-diagonal approximations like KFAC, and conjugate-gradient solvers highlights multiple sources of approximation error that interact with mini-batching. In this paper we (i) show that mini-batch bias introduces a systematic error, (ii) provide a theoretical explanation for this bias in the context of stochastic curvature estimates and classical second-order approximations, (iii) discuss its relevance for second-order optimization and Laplace-based uncertainty quantification in deep networks, and (iv) develop and evaluate debiasing strategies. Our work situates these findings within existing approximations and optimization practice, and we empirically illustrate the effects on representative models and tasks.

title: An Optimal Discriminator Weighted Imitation Perspective for Reinforcement Learning
submission: We propose Iterative Dual Reinforcement Learning (IDRL), which frames offline RL as an optimal discriminator-weighted imitation problem and iteratively refines the visitation distribution ratio. IDRL uses a correction step to approach an optimal ratio without access to additional expert data: at each iteration we remove zero-weight transitions using the previously learned ratio and run Dual-RL on the remaining subdataset, producing a curriculum of improved visitation distributions. We empirically evaluate IDRL on a range of offline datasets including D4RL and corrupted demonstrations and observe improved stability and performance in our runs. We do not provide extensive baseline comparisons here, and the broader significance of the approach for varied environments remains tentative, but the iterative discriminator-weighted viewpoint offers a potentially useful perspective for future work.

title: Warm Diffusion: Recipe for Blur-Noise Mixture Diffusion Models
submission: Diffusion probabilistic models have achieved strong results in generative tasks across diverse data types. Recent work has explored degradations beyond Gaussian noise; here we bridge two diffusion paradigms: hot diffusion, which relies primarily on noise, and cold diffusion, which uses only blurring. We argue that hot diffusion can fail to exploit correlations between high-frequency detail and low-frequency structure, producing random behaviors in early generation steps, while cold diffusion leverages correlations but may neglect the role of randomness, leading to out-of-manifold artifacts. To combine both strengths, we propose Warm Diffusion, a Blur-Noise Mixture Diffusion Model (BNMD) that jointly controls blurring and noise. Our divide-and-conquer strategy exploits spectral dependency in images, disentangling denoising and deblurring to simplify score estimation, and we analyze the Blur-to-Noise Ratio (BNR) via spectral analysis to study trade-offs in learning dynamics and manifold changes. Empirical results on standard benchmarks indicate modest improvements in some settings and suggest directions for further study.

title: GETS: Ensemble Temperature Scaling for Calibration in Graph Neural Networks
submission: Graph Neural Networks deliver strong classification results but often suffer from poor calibration. We propose Graph Ensemble Temperature Scaling (GETS), a calibration framework that combines input and model ensemble strategies within a Graph Mixture-of-Experts architecture. GETS integrates diverse inputs, including logits, node features, and degree embeddings, and uses a set of experts to adaptively select relevant information for calibration. The method is built around a mixture mechanism that weights experts per node. We evaluate GETS on multiple GNN benchmarks and observe improvements in calibration metrics compared to some baselines. The paper discusses computational cost and scalability. While the approach indicates potential for improved calibration, the precise gains depend on dataset and model choices and are modest in several cases. Implementation is available at https://github.com/ZhuangDingyi/GETS/.

title: UNIP: Rethinking Pre-trained Attention Patterns for Infrared Semantic Segmentation
submission: Pre-training substantially improves semantic segmentation when training data is scarce, but the large domain gap between pre-training (e.g., RGB) and fine-tuning (e.g., infrared) is underexplored. We benchmark infrared segmentation performance of various pre-training methods and uncover patterns distinct from the RGB domain. A layerwise analysis of pre-trained attention maps reveals three typical attention patterns—local, hybrid, and global—while pre-training tasks shift pattern distributions across layers. The hybrid pattern attends to both nearby and foreground elements and appears important for segmentation, and a texture bias seems to hinder generalization to infrared. Motivated by these insights, we propose UNIP, a UNified Infrared Pre-training framework that focuses on preserving hybrid attention during pre-training, uses a mixed infrared dataset for pre-training, and applies a feature pyramid refinement at fine-tuning. Experiments indicate notable improvements on infrared segmentation tasks, and UNIP shows promise for broader modalities, though further validation across more datasets is warranted. Code: https://github.com/casiatao/UNIP.

title: Conditional Diffusion with Ordinal Regression: Longitudinal Data Generation for Neurodegenerative Disease Studies
submission: We present a conditional generative approach for synthesizing longitudinal sequences for neurodegenerative disease studies, conditioned on multiple time-dependent ordinal factors such as age and disease severity. Our method sequentially generates continuous trajectories by bridging gaps between sparse visits using a diffusion process, while modeling cohort-level representations with an ordinal regression intended to capture monotonic longitudinal behavior. We conducted experiments on several AD biomarkers; the results, however, are mixed and do not uniformly support all claimed benefits. Some qualitative examples show plausible interpolation, but the quantitative gains are inconclusive and leave open questions about practical applicability and robustness across biomarkers.

title: Batch normalization is sufficient for universal function approximation in CNNs
submission: Normalization techniques, with Batch Normalization (BN) a popular choice, are integral to many deep learning architectures and strongly contribute to learning success. We provide a partial explanation by proving that training only normalization parameters is sufficient for universal function approximation in convolutional neural networks, provided the number of available, potentially random features matches or exceeds the weight parameters of the target networks. In fact, our results show that BN parameters alone suffice for essentially all practical CNNs, with and without residual connections and for almost arbitrary activation functions including ReLU. Our bound on required features improves on recent results for fully-connected networks and resolves the depth-width trade-off driven by architectural constraints. Our explicit construction demonstrates why switching off entire neurons can provide representational benefits. These findings settle the role of BN in representation power and suggest that, with enough random features, training convolutional networks reduces to tuning normalization parameters, dramatically simplifying the learning problem. We validate the theory by matching target networks using a sufficient number of random features.

title: Faithful and Efficient Explanations for Neural Networks via Neural Tangent Kernel Surrogate Models
submission: A recent trend in explainable AI research has focused on surrogate modeling, where neural networks are approximated as simpler ML algorithms such as kernel machines. A second trend has been to utilize kernel functions in various explain-by-example or data attribution tasks. In this work, we combine these two trends to analyze approximate empirical neural tangent kernels (eNTK) for data attribution. Approximation is critical for eNTK analysis due to the high computational cost to compute the eNTK. We define new approximate eNTK and perform novel analysis on how well the resulting kernel machine surrogate models correlate with the underlying neural network. We introduce two new random projection variants of approximate eNTK which allow users to tune the time and memory complexity of their calculation. We conclude that kernel machines using approximate neural tangent kernel as the kernel function are effective surrogate models, with the introduced trace NTK the most consistent performer.

title: Conversational Drug Editing Using Retrieval and Domain Feedback
submission: Recent advancements in conversational large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, have shown promise in domains including drug discovery. However, most prior work focuses on chemical reactions and retrosynthesis while drug editing, a critical step in the discovery pipeline, remains underexplored. To address this, we introduce ChatDrug, a framework to facilitate systematic investigation of drug editing with LLMs. ChatDrug combines a prompt module, a retrieval and domain feedback module, and a conversation module to streamline drug editing workflows. We empirically evaluate ChatDrug across 39 drug editing tasks spanning small molecules, peptides, and proteins and observe strong performance and diverse, valid editing suggestions. Through several case studies, ChatDrug identifies salient substructures for manipulation and provides domain-aware explanations that can aid interpretability and decision-making.

PIORF uses Ollivier–Ricci curvature (ORC) to identify bottleneck regions and then connects these regions with nodes in high-velocity-gradient areas. Implementation details and limitations are also discussed.
