title: GameArena: Evaluating LLM Reasoning through Live Computer Games
submission: Evaluating the reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs) is challenging. Existing benchmarks often depend on static datasets, which are vulnerable to data contamination and may saturate over time, or on binary live human feedback that mixes reasoning with other abilities. As a dynamic alternative, we introduce GameArena, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLM reasoning through interactive gameplay with humans. GameArena consists of three games intended to elicit specific reasoning behaviors (e.g., deductive and inductive patterns) while keeping participants engaged. We collect gaming interactions and analyze them retrospectively to explore LLM decision processes and to annotate stepwise behavior. We gathered a corpus of sessions and participant feedback and provide descriptive assessments for several contemporary LLMs. The contribution is primarily a reusable interactive data source and a set of protocols; detailed claims about broad improvements in evaluation granularity remain preliminary.

title: Learning the Complexity of Weakly Noisy Quantum States
submission: Quantifying the complexity of quantum states is a longstanding topic across quantum computing and theoretical physics. Prior work has established lower bounds on pure state complexity. In this paper we explore the complexity of weakly noisy quantum states via quantum learning methods. We present an efficient learning algorithm that leverages a classical shadow representation of target states to predict circuit complexity for weakly noisy states. The algorithm is designed to be sample-efficient with polynomial classical processing time. We give proofs related to sample complexity and discuss implications for relating learning algorithms to quantum state complexity. Several technical lemmas and algorithmic steps are provided, followed by sketches of proofs and discussion of how the approach might apply in noisy settings. The work highlights connections between learning algorithms and intrinsic properties of quantum states, leaving detailed extensions to future work.

title: Generalizable Human Gaussians from Single-View Image
submission: We address learning 3D human Gaussians from a single image with the goal of recovering appearance and geometry, including regions not directly observed. We propose a single-view generalizable Human Gaussian Model (HGM) that follows a generate-then-refine philosophy guided by human priors and diffusion priors. The pipeline is intended to produce coarse human Gaussians, then refine them using an auxiliary image-based refinement stage. A ControlNet-like component is mentioned to refine rendered back-view images, and a dual-branch design incorporates SMPL-X body priors to constrain plausible poses and shapes. Because initial SMPL-X estimates can be imperfect, HGM is designed to progressively update those priors during processing. We validate the approach on public datasets and observe improvements in novel view consistency and surface quality in many cases, while noting that some failure modes remain when priors are inaccurate or generation is ambiguous.

submission: The ability of an agent to do well in new environments is a critical aspect of intelligence. In machine learning, this ability is known as strong or out-of-distribution generalization. title: HADAMRNN: BINARY AND SPARSE TERNARY ORTHOGONAL RNNS
submission: Binary and sparse ternary weights enable faster computations and lighter representations for edge devices, yet vanilla RNNs are highly sensitive to changes in their recurrent weights, making binarization and ternarization challenging. To date, no method has successfully achieved binarization or ternarization of vanilla RNN weights. We present a new approach leveraging properties of Hadamard matrices to parameterize a subset of binary and sparse ternary orthogonal matrices. This parameterization enables training orthogonal RNNs (ORNNs) with binary and sparse ternary recurrent weights, producing a specific class of binary and sparse ternary vanilla RNNs. The resulting ORNNs, called HadamRNN and Block-HadamRNN, are evaluated on the copy task, permuted and sequential MNIST tasks, and IMDB. Despite binarization or sparse ternarization, these RNNs maintain performance comparable to full-precision models in our tests. Notably, this approach is the first with binary recurrent weights capable of tackling the copy task over 1000 timesteps, though further analysis of limitations and stability remains necessary.

title: On Discriminative Probabilistic Modeling for Self-Supervised Representation Learning
submission: We study discriminative probabilistic modeling on a continuous domain for the data prediction task in (multimodal) self-supervised representation learning. To avoid the prohibitive integral computation in the partition function for each anchor, we leverage multiple importance sampling (MIS) for Monte Carlo integration and show InfoNCE-like contrastive losses arise as special cases. Within this framework, we conduct generalization error analysis that suggests limitations of current InfoNCE-based contrastive loss and provides directions to reduce Monte Carlo integration error. Motivated by these insights, we propose a non-parametric approximation for the sum of conditional probability densities required by MIS via convex optimization, and an efficient algorithm to solve the resulting objective. Empirical comparisons on CC3M and CC12M indicate our algorithm can outperform representative baselines in some settings, but further work is needed to firmly establish when and why the proposed objective consistently improves representation learning.

title: RRM:  Robust Reward Model Training Mitigates Reward Hacking
submission: Reward models (RMs) are central to aligning large language models with human preferences. However traditional RM training that uses response pairs tied to particular prompts struggles to disentangle prompt-driven preferences from prompt-independent artifacts such as response length and format. In this work we expose this limitation: RMs often cannot effectively distinguish contextual signals from irrelevant artifacts when inferring preferences. To address it we introduce a causal framework to learn preferences that are independent of these artifacts and propose a data augmentation technique intended to remove them. Extensive experiments show our method filters out undesirable artifacts, yielding a more robust reward model (RRM). Our RRM improves a pairwise reward model trained on Gemma-2-9b-it on Reward-Bench, increasing accuracy from 80.61% to 84.15%. We also train two DPO policies using both RM and RRM, and observe improved MT-Bench scores (7.27 to 8.31) and length-controlled win-rates in AlpacaEval-2 (33.46% to 52.49%). Some evaluation cases however remain less clear and warrant follow-up.

submission: Recent advances in large language models increased their context windows, but long-term memory management remains challenging. We introduce MemTree, an algorithm that uses a dynamic, tree-structured memory representation to organize, retrieve, and integrate information, somewhat like human schemas. title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization Through the Data-Centric Lens
submission: The weak-to-strong generalization phenomenon drives data-efficient learning and related applications such as superalignment. Despite many algorithmic advances, it remains unclear which properties of data enable weak-to-strong transitions. We propose a data-centric mechanism, the overlap density, to characterize weak-to-strong generalization. Intuitively, generalization appears to track how many points contain overlaps—both easy patterns learnable by a weak model and harder patterns that require a stronger model—because such points allow weak predictions to inform learning of challenging patterns. To operationalize this idea we describe a practical overlap detection procedure to estimate overlap density from data and outline a simple selection strategy to choose among multiple data sources to increase overlap density. We also present a theoretical statement linking generalization benefit to overlap density and a regret-style bound for the selection strategy. Empirical illustrations across a variety of settings are provided to support the proposed mechanism, though detailed limitations and broader impacts remain to be fully explored.

title: Group Downsampling with Equivariant Anti-aliasing
submission: Downsampling layers are crucial building blocks in CNN architectures, which help to increase the receptive field for learning high-level features and reduce the amount of memory/computation in the model. In this work, we study the generalization of the uniform downsampling layer for group equivariant architectures, e.g., $G$-CNNs. That is, we aim to downsample signals (feature maps) on general finite groups *with* anti-aliasing. This involves the following: **(a)** Given a finite group and a downsampling rate, we present an algorithm to form a suitable choice of subgroup.  **(b)** Given a group and a subgroup, we study the notion of bandlimited-ness and propose how to perform anti-aliasing. Notably, our method generalizes the notion of downsampling based on classical sampling theory. When the signal is on a cyclic group, i.e., periodic, our method recovers the standard downsampling of an ideal low-pass filter followed by a subsampling operation. Finally, we conducted experiments on image classification tasks demonstrating that the proposed downsampling operation improves accuracy, better preserves equivariance, and reduces model size when incorporated into $G$-equivariant networks

submission: Bayesian optimization (BO) provides an efficient approach to optimize expensive black-box functions using Gaussian process priors and acquisition functions. Extending recent learning-based acquisition strategies to multi-objective BO (MOBO) is challenging due to non-Markovian dependencies and hypervolume identifiability. We present BOFormer, a generalized deep Q-learning framework that operationalizes non-Markovian decision-making via sequence modeling with Transformers. BOFormer is trained to select evaluation points by conditioning on histories of observations and is framed as a sequence prediction problem. In experiments we compare BOFormer against common rule-based and learned baselines: the evaluation focuses on standard synthetic multi-objective tasks as well as hyperparameter tuning benchmarks, and reports qualitative improvements in search efficiency. While the method is motivated by non-Markovian RL theory and sequence modeling, the empirical section concentrates on aggregate optimization curves from single-objective baselines, leaving some aspects of the intended multi-objective evaluation less directly tied to the algorithmic description.

submission: We tackle creating 3D assets for household articulated objects from a single image. title: A Decade's Battle on Dataset Bias: Are We There Yet?
submission: We revisit the “dataset classification” experiment suggested by Torralba & Efros (2011) in the present era of large-scale, diverse datasets and more capable neural architectures. Surprisingly, modern neural networks can achieve high accuracy in classifying which dataset an image is from: e.g., we report 84.7% accuracy on held-out validation data for a three-way problem consisting of the YFCC, CC, and DataComp datasets. Additional experiments indicate that such a dataset classifier can learn semantic features that transfer to other tasks and are not explained solely by memorization. However, the scope and implications of this finding are limited: dataset-identification ability depends on dataset composition and training setup, and further work is required to understand how these observations should influence dataset collection and benchmarking practices.

title: Constrained Bi-Level Optimization: Proximal Lagrangian Value Function Approach and Hessian-free Algorithm
submission: This paper presents a new approach and algorithm for solving a class of constrained Bi-Level Optimization (BLO) problems in which the lower-level problem involves constraints coupling both upper-level and lower-level variables. Such problems have recently gained significant attention due to their broad applicability in machine learning. However, conventional gradient-based methods unavoidably rely on computationally intensive calculations related to the Hessian matrix. To address this challenge, we devise a smooth proximal Lagrangian value function to handle the constrained lower-level problem. Utilizing this construct, we introduce a single-level reformulation for constrained BLOs that transforms the original BLO problem into an equivalent optimization problem with smooth constraints. Enabled by this reformulation, we develop a Hessian-free gradient-based algorithm—termed proximal Lagrangian Value function-based Hessian-free Bi-level Algorithm (LV-HBA)—that is straightforward to implement in a single loop manner. Consequently, LV-HBA is especially well-suited for machine learning applications. Furthermore, we offer non-asymptotic convergence analysis for LV-HBA, eliminating the need for traditional strong convexity assumptions for the lower-level problem while also being capable of accommodating non-singleton scenarios. Empirical results substantiate the algorithm's superior practical performance.

title: Towards Effective Evaluations and Comparisons for LLM Unlearning Methods
submission: The imperative to eliminate undesirable data memorization underscores the significance of machine unlearning for large language models (LLMs). Recent research has introduced a series of promising unlearning methods, boosting the practical significance of the field. title: Efficient Degradation-agnostic Image Restoration via Channel-Wise Functional Decomposition and Manifold Regularization
submission: Degradation-agnostic image restoration aims to handle diverse corruptions with a unified model, yet balancing efficiency and performance across degradations remains challenging. We present MIRAGE, an efficient framework built around two ideas. First, a channel-wise functional decomposition repurposes channel redundancy in attention by assigning CNN, attention, and MLP branches to local textures, global context, and channel statistics respectively. This decomposition encourages degradation-agnostic learning while improving efficiency when compared to a single monolithic design. Second, manifold regularization performs cross-layer contrastive alignment in Symmetric Positive Definite (SPD) space to improve feature consistency across corruptions. We describe implementation details and ablations showing architectural trade-offs and efficiency considerations. MIRAGE is designed to be scalable and generalizable to unseen corruptions. While we do not exhaustively benchmark against every prior approach here, the framework is intended as a practical, efficient alternative for all-in-one image restoration.

title: Text-to-3D by Stitching a Multi-view Reconstruction Network to a Video Generator
submission: The rapid progress of large, pretrained models for both visual content generation and 3D reconstruction opens up new possibilities for text-to-3D generation. Intuitively, one could obtain a formidable 3D scene generator if one were able to combine the power of a modern latent text-to-video model as "generator" with the geometric abilities of a recent (feedforward) 3D reconstruction system as "decoder". We introduce **VIST3A**, a general framework that does just that, addressing two main challenges. First, the two components must be joined in a way that preserves the rich knowledge encoded in their weights. We revisit *model stitching*, i.e., we identify the layer in the 3D decoder that best matches the latent representation produced by the text-to-video generator and stitch the two parts together. That operation requires only a small dataset and no labels. Second, the text-to-video generator must be aligned with the stitched 3D decoder, to ensure that the generated latents are decodable into consistent, perceptually convincing 3D scene geometry. To that end, we adapt *direct reward finetuning*, a popular technique for human preference alignment. We evaluate the proposed VIST3A approach with different video generators and 3D reconstruction models. All tested pairings markedly improve over prior text-to-3D models that output Gaussian splats. Moreover, by choosing a suitable 3D base model, VIST3A also enables high-quality text-to-pointmap generation.

title: EditLens: Quantifying the Extent of AI Editing in Text
submission: Many prompts to large language models request edits to user-provided text rather than fresh generation. We show that AI-edited text is distinguishable from both purely human and fully AI-generated text. First, we propose lightweight similarity metrics to quantify the magnitude of AI editing given an original human draft, and validate these metrics with human annotators. Using these similarity metrics as intermediate supervision, we train EditLens, a regression model that predicts the amount of AI editing in a text. Our model attains strong classification performance on human/AI/mixed distinctions (reported F1=94.7% binary, 90.4% ternary) and shows the ability to regress editing magnitude. We further analyze AI edits applied by a popular writing assistance tool as a case study. While the high-level approach and evaluation show promise, the manuscript focuses on the metric design and model evaluation results rather than exhaustive methodological exposition.

title: Expressive yet Efficient Feature Expansion with Adaptive Cross-Hadamard Products
submission: Recent theoretical advances reveal that the Hadamard product induces nonlinear representations and implicit high-dimensional mappings for deep learning, yet their practical deployment in resource-constrained vision models remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce the Adaptive Cross-Hadamard (ACH) module, a novel operator that embeds learnability through differentiable discrete sampling and dynamic softsign normalization. This facilitates highly efficient feature reuse without incurring additional convolutional parameters, while ensuring stable gradient flow. Integrated into Hadaptive-Net (Hadamard Adaptive Network) via neural architecture search, our approach is designed to achieve unprecedented efficiency. We describe the operator, its integration into a lightweight architecture, and training considerations. The paper argues for Hadamard operations as concrete building blocks for efficient vision models and discusses possible applications and deployment scenarios, leaving comprehensive empirical evaluation and full experimental results to future work.

title: Spotlight on Token Perception for Multimodal Reinforcement Learning
submission: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has improved multimodal reasoning for large vision-language models, yet visual perception within RLVR optimization is underexplored. We introduce token perception as a measure of visual dependency for each generated token and analyze Chain-of-Thought rollouts to reveal two observations: token perception is sparsely distributed across tokens, and different trajectories vary widely in overall visual dependency. Motivated by these observations, we propose Visually-Perceptive Policy Optimization (VPPO), a policy gradient algorithm that reweights trajectory advantages by overall visual dependency and focuses updates on perceptually pivotal tokens. We evaluate VPPO on a suite of perception and reasoning tasks and report consistent improvements across multiple model scales. The paper argues for a token-level perceptual perspective to better align multimodal policy updates with visual grounding, though the precise mechanisms and limitations warrant further analysis.

submission: Recent neural solvers have made progress on vehicle routing problems (VRPs), yet many of them assume symmetric Euclidean distances, limiting applicability to real-world asymmetric scenarios. In this paper, we propose RADAR, a neural framework intended to augment neural VRP solvers to better handle asymmetric inputs. Owing to space constraints, methodological specifics and empirical results are omitted here; instead, we provide a roadmap for implementing RADAR components and directions for validating the approach on synthetic and real-world asymmetric VRP benchmarks.

submission: Generalized linear bandits have been extensively studied due to their broad applicability in real-world online decision-making problems. PDDLLM constructs domains and integrates them with motion planners to produce executable plans, enhancing long-horizon planning automation. Across a broad set of tasks and environments, PDDLLM demonstrates improved reliability, reduced token costs, and successful deployment on physical robot platforms, illustrating the practical value of automated domain derivation.

submission: Modeling multi-type event sequences with marked temporal point processes (MTPPs) provides a principled framework for uncovering governing dynamical rules and predicting future events. We pursue a fundamentally different strategy: leveraging amortized inference and in-context learning, we pretrain a deep neural network to infer, *in-context*, the conditional intensity functions of event histories from a context consisting of sets of event sequences. Pretraining is performed on a large synthetic dataset of MTPPs sampled from a broad distribution over point processes. Once pretrained, our Foundation Inference Model for Point Processes (FIM-PP) can estimate MTPPs from real-world data without additional training, or be rapidly finetuned to specific target systems. Across common benchmark datasets, FIM-PP matches the performance of specialized models in *zero-shot mode*. After only a few finetuning iterations, FIM-PP further improves its predictions and *outperforms competing methods on the majority of evaluated tasks*.

submission: Adversarial attacks on Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) often fail to transfer well to black-box targets or produce perceptible artifacts. We present Progressive Semantic Infusion (PSI), a diffusion-based attack that progressively aligns adversarial examples with target semantics. title: SK2Decompile: LLM-based Two-Phase Binary Decompilation from Skeleton to Skin
submission:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising approach for binary decompilation. However, the existing LLM-based decompilers still are somewhat limited in effectively presenting a program's source-level structure with its original identifiers.
To mitigate this, we introduce SK2Decompile, a novel two-phase approach to decompile from the skeleton (semantic structure) to the skin (identifier) of programs. Specifically, we first apply a Structure Recovery model to translate a program's binary code to an Intermediate Representation (IR) as deriving the program's "skeleton", i.e., preserving control flow and data structures while obfuscating all identifiers with generic placeholders. We also apply reinforcement learning to reward the model for producing program structures that adhere to the syntactic and semantic rules expected by compilers. Second, we apply an Identifier Naming model to produce meaningful identifiers which reflect actual program semantics as deriving the program's "skin". We train the Identifier Naming model with a separate reinforcement learning objective that rewards the semantic similarity between its predictions and the reference code. Such a two-phase decompilation process facilitates advancing the correctness and readability of decompilation independently.
Our evaluations indicate that SK2Decompile, significantly outperforms the SOTA baselines, achieving 21.6% average re-executability rate gain over GPT-5-mini on the HumanEval dataset and 29.4% average R2I improvement over Idioms on the GitHub2025 benchmark.

title: VoMP: Predicting Volumetric Mechanical Property Fields
submission: Physical simulation relies on spatially-varying mechanical properties, typically laboriously hand-crafted. We present the first feed-forward model to predict fine-grained mechanical properties, Young’s modulus ($E$), Poisson’s ratio ($\nu$), and density ($\rho$), throughout *the volume* of 3D objects. Our model supports any 3D representation that can be rendered and voxelized, including Signed Distance Fields (SDFs), Gaussian Splats and Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). To achieve this, we aggregate per-voxel multi-view features for any input, which are passed to our trained Geometry Transformer to predict per-voxel material latent codes. These latents reside on the trained manifold of physically plausible materials, which we train on a real-world dataset, guaranteeing the validity of decoded per-voxel materials. To obtain object-level training data, we propose an annotation pipeline combining knowledge from segmented 3D datasets, material databases, and a vision-language model. Experiments show that VoMP estimates accurate volumetric properties and can convert 3D objects into simulation-ready assets, resulting in realistic deformable simulations and far outperforming prior art.

title: Motion-R1: Enhancing Motion Generation with Decomposed Chain-of-Thought and RL Binding
submission: Text-to-motion generation has advanced but still faces challenges in capturing temporal and causal structure and in keeping RL-based pipelines practical. We introduce Motion-R1, a framework that combines a decomposed Chain-of-Thought style reasoning pipeline with reinforcement learning to improve motion quality and interpretability. Motion-R1 centers on a Decomposed CoT Data Engine that synthesizes reasoning data through an automated pipeline so the model can supposedly better represent temporal dependencies, and an RL Binding component that incorporates multimodal text-motion alignment into the reward to guide generation. The approach is intended to make motions more semantically accurate and motionally realistic while remaining scalable. We report improvements over prior methods on standard motion datasets across a range of metrics, arguing that Motion-R1 better handles complex generation tasks — though our objective is to provide a flexible hybrid that can be adapted to different pipelines.

title: TESSAR: Geometry-Aware Active Regression via Dynamic Voronoi Tessellation
submission: Active learning improves efficiency by selectively querying informative samples, but adapting these ideas to regression is challenging because informative signal is spread across the dataset rather than concentrated near a decision boundary. Distance-based sampling promotes diversity but can overemphasize peripheral regions while missing dense interior regions that are informative. We propose TESSAR, a tessellation-based sampling framework that leverages geometric structure for active regression. Central to the proposal is a Voronoi-derived score intended to capture interior coverage, peripheral exploration, and representativity. Intuitively, the method uses tessellation to identify regions where model disagreement or representativity suggest informative samples. TESSAR unifies these considerations into a single acquisition score and is designed to be broadly applicable to regression tasks. While the framework promises improved sample efficiency and a principled geometric view of selection, this abstract focuses on the conceptual formulation rather than a detailed methodology or experimental quantification.

title: Modeling the Density of Pixel-level Self-supervised Embeddings for Unsupervised Pathology Segmentation in Medical CT
submission: Detecting all pathological findings in 3D medical images is challenging because supervised models only see a few annotated pathology classes. We frame pathology detection as unsupervised visual anomaly segmentation (UVAS), leveraging the rarity of pathological patterns relative to healthy anatomy. We enhance the density-based UVAS framework with two innovations: dense self-supervised learning for feature extraction, removing the need for supervised pretraining, and learned masking-invariant dense features as conditioning variables instead of hand-crafted positional encodings. Trained on over 30,000 unlabeled 3D CT volumes, our fully self-supervised model Screener is intended to improve anomaly segmentation. We evaluate on several large-scale test datasets and report improved performance compared to prior work; in low-shot supervised fine-tuning Screener also aims to provide a strong foundation for pathology segmentation. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/mishgon/screener.

title: From Single to Multi-Granularity: Toward Long-Term Memory Association and Selection of Conversational Agents
submission: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely adopted in conversational agents. As interactions lengthen, dialogues accumulate extensive records and context-window limits make it hard to maintain coherent long-term memory and personalization. Retrieval-augmented memory systems have emerged, but many rely on single-granularity segmentation and retrieval which, as commonly argued, fails to capture deep memory connections. To tackle these limits, we propose MemGAS, a framework that claims to enhance memory consolidation by constructing multi-granularity association, adaptive selection, and retrieval. MemGAS is based on multi-granularity memory units and employs Gaussian Mixture Models to cluster and associate new memories with historical ones. An entropy-based router is used to select granularity by evaluating query relevance distributions and balancing completeness and noise. Retrieved memories are further refined via LLM-based filtering. Experiments on several long-term memory benchmarks indicate improvements over existing methods, though the core problem formulation and some motivations are left underspecified in places.

title: STAR: Strategy-driven Automatic Jailbreak Red-teaming For Large Language Model
submission: Jailbreaking techniques aim to bypass LLM safety alignment; automated red-teaming is crucial for vulnerability discovery. Most existing methods search text space and tend to generate semantically similar prompts, limiting exploration of latent vulnerabilities. We present STAR (Strategy-driven Automatic Jailbreak Red-teaming), a black-box framework that shifts strategy exploration into the model's latent activation space. STAR has two modules: a strategy generation module that extracts principal components of known strategies and recombines them to produce novel abstract strategies, and a prompt generation module that maps these strategies into concrete jailbreak prompts. Experiments show that STAR finds a diverse set of jailbreaks and achieves higher attack rates in selected settings compared to prior automated methods. While promising for comprehensive security evaluation, the results are context-dependent and further study is needed to understand limits and potential defensive countermeasures.

submission: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) show remarkable capabilities yet they sometimes overthink or underthink; overthinking wastes compute on easy items, underthinking fails to explore enough reasoning paths. ReBalance uses confidence as a continuous indicator, detects overthinking via variance and underthinking via consistent overconfidence, aggregates hidden states into reasoning mode prototypes, and computes a steering vector to guide trajectories. We evaluate across four models (0.5B–32B) and nine benchmarks in math, QA, and coding and claim reduced redundancy and improved accuracy. The discussion mixes conceptual motivations and method elements without a clear problem statement or a crisp separation of why this approach is preferable in specific deployment settings.

title: Text2Arch: A Dataset for Generating Scientific Architecture Diagrams from Natural Language Descriptions
submission: Communicating complex system designs or scientific processes through text alone is inefficient and prone to ambiguity. A system that automatically generates scientific architecture diagrams from text with high semantic fidelity can be useful in multiple applications like enterprise architecture visualization, AI-driven software design, and educational content creation. Hence, in this paper, we focus on leveraging language models to perform semantic understanding of the input text description to generate intermediate code that can be processed to generate high-fidelity architecture diagrams. Unfortunately, no clean large-scale open-access dataset exists, implying lack of any effective open models for this task. Hence, we contribute a comprehensive dataset, \system, comprising scientific architecture images, their corresponding textual descriptions, and associated DOT code representations.  Leveraging this resource, we fine-tune a suite of small language models, and also perform in-context learning using GPT-4o. Through extensive experimentation, we show that \system{} models significantly outperform existing baseline models like DiagramAgent and perform at par with in-context learning based generations from GPT-4o. We have added code and data as Supplementary material, and will make them (and models) publicly available on acceptance.

submission: Inspired by behavioral science, we propose Behavior Learning (BL), a novel general-purpose machine learning framework that learns interpretable and identifiable optimization structures from data, ranging from single optimization problems to hierarchical compositions. It unifies predictive performance, intrinsic interpretability, and identifiability, with broad applicability to scientific domains involving optimization. BL parameterizes a compositional utility function built from intrinsically interpretable modular blocks, which induces a data distribution for prediction and generation. title: ExpVid: A Benchmark for Experiment Video Understanding & Reasoning
submission: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) hold promise for accelerating scientific discovery by interpreting complex experimental procedures. ExpVid not only provides a diagnostic tool but also charts a roadmap for developing MLLMs capable of becoming trustworthy partners in scientific experimentation.

title: AlignFlow: Improving Flow-based Generative Models with Semi-Discrete Optimal Transport
submission: Flow-based generative models (FGMs) transform simple noise into complex data distributions, and coupling them with optimal transport (OT) can yield straighter flow trajectories and more effective inference. Existing OT-FGM methods, however, estimate plans from minibatches which limits scalability. We propose AlignFlow, which leverages semi-discrete optimal transport (SDOT) to establish an explicit, optimal alignment between the continuous noise distribution and data points via Laguerre cell partitioning of the noise space. During training, i.i.d. noise samples are deterministically paired to data points through the SDOT map. AlignFlow is a plug-and-play component with negligible overhead and, in our experiments, produces universally superior performance across a wide range of state-of-the-art FGM algorithms and datasets, often yielding markedly better sample quality and likelihood. We release code to encourage adoption and replication.

title: Operator Theory-Driven Autoformulation of MDPs for Control of Queueing Systems
submission: Autoformulation has used LLMs to translate natural-language decision problems into formal mathematical programs, but sequential decision-making settings modeled as Markov decision processes (MDPs) introduce unique challenges. We focus on queueing problems and propose an operator-theoretic autoformulation framework that represents the Bellman equation as a graph of interpretable operators, each corresponding to events such as arrival, departure, or routing. We argue this approach automatically reveals interpretable policy structure and, in practice, yields fast downstream solutions for classical queueing formulations. We believe this operator view provides a general-purpose bridge from language descriptions to MDP formulations.

title: Attention Sinks and Compression Valleys in LLMs are Two Sides of the Same Coin
submission: Attention sinks and compression valleys have been studied separately; here we connect them, attributing both to the emergence of massive activations in the residual stream. We provide theoretical arguments that large activation norms induce representational compression and derive bounds on the accompanying entropy reduction. Empirically, across several models (≈410M–120B parameters), we observe that when the beginning-of-sequence token develops extreme activation norms in middle layers, compression valleys and attention sinks tend to co-occur. Targeted ablations are broadly consistent with the theoretical predictions. Building on these observations, we propose the Mix-Compress-Refine theory as a tentative framework: (1) broad mixing early, (2) compressed computation with limited mixing in the middle, and (3) selective refinement later. While this unified view helps interpret certain layerwise task differences, the theory remains preliminary and calls for further empirical and theoretical validation.

submission: Post-training multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer promise for interactive agents in computer use, web navigation, and robotics, but scaling post-training requires diverse, feasible, and verifiable downstream task datasets. Existing task generation methods depend heavily on human annotation or limited prompting of MLLMs with sparse environment information, which scales poorly. We present AutoPlay, a pipeline that seeks to generate environment-grounded tasks by explicitly exploring interactive environments and synthesizing tasks from the discovered interactions. AutoPlay operates in two broad phases: an exploration phase where an MLLM-based explorer uncovers novel states and functionalities, and a task generation phase where a generator synthesizes diverse, executable, verifiable tasks from exploration traces and guideline prompts. Using AutoPlay we generate large collections of tasks across mobile and desktop environments and use them to synthesize demonstrations with an MLLM executor and verifier. These synthetic tasks and demonstrations improve training of UI agents, yielding measurable gains in success rates and enabling reinforcement learning with verifier-based rewards. Details of the exploration heuristics and generator architecture are omitted here but remain central to future refinement.

submission: Collaborative perception integrates multi-agent perspectives to enhance sensing range and reduce occlusion. We present SiMO (Single-Modality-Operable Multimodal Collaborative Perception), which aims to be robust when a key sensor like LiDAR is unavailable. By adopting a Length-Adaptive Multi-Modal Fusion (LAMMA) scheme, SiMO attempts to handle remaining modal features during modal failures while preserving a consistent semantic space. title: The Limits of Inference Scaling Through Resampling
submission: Inference scaling via resampling—repeatedly sampling until a verifier accepts—has been proposed to let weaker models approximate stronger ones. We analyze limits of this idea when verifiers are imperfect and can output false positives. title: Multi-Condition Conformal Selection
submission: Selecting high-quality candidates from large-scale datasets is critically important in resource-constrained applications such as drug discovery, precision medicine, and the alignment of large language models. While conformal selection methods offer a rigorous solution with False Discovery Rate (FDR) control, their applicability is confined to single-threshold scenarios (i.e., y > c) and overlooks practical needs for multi-condition selection, such as conjunctive or disjunctive conditions.  In this work, we propose the Multi-Condition Conformal Selection (MCCS) algorithm, which extends conformal selection to scenarios with multiple conditions. In particular, we introduce a novel nonconformity score with regional monotonicity for conjunctive conditions and a global Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) procedure for disjunctive conditions, thereby establishing finite-sample FDR control with theoretical guarantees. The integration of these components enables the proposed method to achieve rigorous FDR-controlled selection in various multi-condition environments. Extensive experiments validate the superiority of MCCS over baselines, its generalizability across diverse condition combinations, different real-world modalities, and multi-task scalability.

title: Boosting Medical Visual Understanding From Multi-Granular Language Learning
submission: Image–text pretraining like CLIP has advanced visual understanding, but single-label, single-granularity alignment limits performance in domains such as medical imaging where images have multiple labels at different granularities. We propose Multi-Granular Language Learning (MGLL), a contrastive framework to improve multi-label and cross-granularity alignment. MGLL leverages structured multi-label supervision, integrates textual descriptions across granularities, and introduces soft-label supervision with point-wise constraints to enhance alignment. It employs smooth KL divergence to enforce cross-granularity consistency while remaining computationally efficient as a plug-and-play module for vision–language models. Pretrained on a large multi-granular dataset we constructed and evaluated across multiple medical imaging benchmarks, MGLL consistently outperforms prior methods in downstream tasks. We argue MGLL substantially advances medical visual understanding and, in practice, makes many previous single-granularity approaches obsolete for multi-label clinical scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/HUANGLIZI/MGLL.

title: DriftLite: Lightweight Drift Control for Inference-Time Scaling of Diffusion Models
submission: We study inference-time scaling for diffusion models: adapting a pre-trained model to a new target distribution without retraining. Guidance-based methods are simple but biased, whereas particle-based corrections can suffer from weight degeneracy and high cost. We introduce DriftLite, a lightweight, training-free particle-based approach that steers inference dynamics on-the-fly by exploiting a degree of freedom in the Fokker–Planck equation between drift and particle potential. DriftLite yields two practical instantiations, Variance- and Energy-Controlling Guidance (VCG/ECG), for approximating an improved drift with modest overhead. We outline theoretical stability properties and describe implementation details. Experiments on Gaussian mixtures, particle systems, and a protein–ligand co-folding setting show some reductions in variance relative to pure guidance; however, empirical outcomes are mixed across tasks and do not uniformly dominate sequential Monte Carlo baselines. These mixed results underscore directions for further refinement of DriftLite and broader evaluation.

title: Beware Untrusted Simulators -- Reward-Free Backdoor Attacks in Reinforcement Learning
submission: Simulated environments are central to reinforcement learning, but they remain a security blind spot because adversarial simulator developers can alter dynamics. We study a novel threat in which simulator dynamics are manipulated to stealthily implant action-level backdoors into RL agents. The implanted backdoor enables an adversary to reliably trigger targeted actions when a predefined trigger appears, potentially causing dangerous behavior. We describe the attack construction, threat model, and training-time modifications that enable stealthy backdoor implantation, and we provide conceptual analysis of transferability to real robotic hardware. We discuss defenses and the need to secure simulator components, though extensive empirical results and formal proofs are left for follow-up work.

title: DeepResearch Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Deep Research Agents
submission: Deep Research Agents (DRAs) are emerging as one of the most practical classes of LLM-based agents. Given an open-ended research task, they find, analyze, and synthesize large numbers of online sources to produce a comprehensive report at the level of a research analyst, which can compress hours of manual desk research into minutes. However, a comprehensive benchmark for systematically evaluating the capabilities of these agents remains absent. To bridge this gap, we introduce DeepResearch Bench, a benchmark consisting of 100 PhD-level research tasks, each meticulously crafted by domain experts across 22 distinct fields. To evaluate DRAs comprehensively, we propose two complementary and fully automated methodologies: the first is a reference-based method with adaptive criteria to assess the quality of generated research reports, and the second evaluates a DRA’s information-retrieval and collection capabilities by assessing its effective citation count and overall citation accuracy. By conducting extensive human consistency experiments, we demonstrate that our evaluation methods are highly aligned with expert judges and faithfully reflect human judgments of quality differences among DRA-generated content. We are open-sourcing DeepResearch Bench and key components of these frameworks to accelerate the development of practical LLM-based agents.

title: SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution?
submission: The common approach to communicate a large language model's (LLM) uncertainty is to add a percentage number or a hedging word to its response. But is this all we can do? Instead of generating a single answer and then hedging it, an LLM that is fully transparent to the user needs to be able to reflect on its internal belief distribution and output a summary of all options it deems possible, and how likely they are. To test whether LLMs possess this capability, we develop the SelfReflect metric, an information-theoretic distance between a given summary and a distribution over answers. In interventional and human studies, we find that SelfReflect indicates even slight deviations, yielding a fine measure of faithfulness between a summary string and an LLM's actual internal distribution over answers. With SelfReflect, we make a resounding negative observation: modern LLMs are, across the board, incapable of revealing what they are uncertain about, neither through reasoning, nor chains-of-thoughts, nor explicit finetuning. However, we do find that LLMs are able to generate faithful summaries of their uncertainties if we help them by sampling multiple outputs and feeding them back into the context. This simple approach shines a light at the universal way of communicating LLM uncertainties whose future development the SelfReflect score enables. To support the development of this universal form of LLM uncertainties, we publish the code that implements our metric for arbitrary LLMs under https://github.com/apple/ml-selfreflect .

title: Knowledge Externalization: Reversible Unlearning and Modular Retrieval in Multimodal Large Language Models
submission: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong cross-modal understanding from web-scale training, but they also internalize sensitive personal and proprietary information. Prior machine unlearning approaches typically alter model weights irreversibly to remove knowledge. We propose Knowledge Externalization, a framework for reversible and modular knowledge management in MLLMs that treats targeted knowledge as an external resource. We introduce Dual-Stream Memory Tuning, which transfers targeted concepts from internal parameters into external memory tokens, and Soft Orthogonal Weighting to reduce gradient interference when externalizing multiple concepts by encouraging token independence. In our experiments the base model shows reduced retention of externalized concepts, and the corresponding memory tokens can be reattached to restore behavior. We also observe that external tokens can be edited after externalization and that combining multiple tokens often recovers the associated concepts. These results suggest a promising direction for auditable, user-controllable knowledge management, though further validation across broader settings is warranted.

title: Hidden Breakthroughs in Language Model Training
submission: Loss curves are smooth during most of model training, so visible discontinuities stand out as possible conceptual breakthroughs. Studying these breakthroughs enables a deeper understanding of learning dynamics, but only when they are properly identified. This paper argues that similar breakthroughs occur frequently throughout training but they are obscured by a loss metric that collapses all variation into a single scalar. To find these hidden transitions, we introduce POLCA, a method for decomposing changes in loss along arbitrary bases of the low-rank training subspace. We use our method to identify clusters of samples that share similar changes in loss during training, disaggregating the overall loss into that of smaller groups of conceptually similar data. We validate our method on synthetic arithmetic and natural language tasks, showing that POLCA recovers clusters that represent interpretable breakthroughs in the model's capabilities. We demonstrate the promise of these hidden phase transitions as a tool for unsupervised interpretability.

title: RelayFormer: A Unified Local-Global Attention Framework for Scalable Image and Video Manipulation Localization
submission: Visual manipulation localization (VML) aims to identify tampered regions in images and videos, a task made more challenging by modern editing tools. Existing methods face two central issues: resolution diversity and the difficulty of extending spatial models to spatio-temporal inputs. Resizing or padding can distort subtle forensic cues and introduce unnecessary cost, and models for images often cannot be straightforwardly adapted to video. To address these, we propose RelayFormer, a unified framework that adapts to varying resolutions and handles both static and temporal visual data. RelayFormer partitions inputs into fixed-size sub-images and introduces Global Local Relay (GLR) tokens that propagate structured context through a relay-based attention mechanism. This enables efficient exchange of global cues while preserving fine-grained manipulation artifacts. Unlike prior approaches that rely on uniform resizing or sparse attention, RelayFormer scales to variable resolutions and video sequences with minimal overhead. Experiments across benchmarks show superior performance and strong efficiency while keeping a favorable balance between accuracy and compute.

title: InfoScan: Information-Efficient Visual Scanning via Resource-Adaptive Walks
submission: High-resolution visual representation learning is hard due to the quadratic cost of Vision Transformers and limitations of efficient alternatives that use fixed scanning patterns. We propose InfoScan, an information-aware scanning mechanism for state-space visual backbones that dynamically allocates compute to salient image regions. title: InfLLM-V2: Dense-Sparse Switchable Attention for Seamless Short-to-Long Adaptation
submission: Long-sequence processing is a critical capability for modern large language models. However, the self-attention mechanism in the standard Transformer architecture faces severe computational and memory bottlenecks when processing long sequences. While trainable sparse attention methods offer a promising solution, existing approaches such as NSA introduce excessive extra parameters and disrupt the conventional pretrain-on-short, finetune-on-long workflow, resulting in slow convergence and difficulty in acceleration. To overcome these limitations, we introduce dense-sparse switchable attention framework, termed as InfLLM-V2. InfLLM-V2 is a trainable sparse attention that seamlessly adapts models from short to long sequences. Specifically, InfLLM-V2 reuses dense attention parameters through parameter-free architecture modification, maintaining consistency between short and long sequence processing. Additionally, InfLLM-V2 ensures computational efficiency across all sequence lengths, by using dense attention for short inputs and smoothly transitioning to sparse attention for long sequences. To achieve practical acceleration, we further introduce an efficient implementation of InfLLM-V2 that significantly reduces the computational overhead. Our experiments on long-context understanding and chain-of-thought reasoning demonstrate that InfLLM-V2 is 4$\times$ faster than dense attention while retaining 98.1\% and 99.7\% of the performance, respectively. Based on the InfLLM-V2 framework, we have trained and open-sourced MiniCPM4.1 (https://huggingface.co/openbmb/MiniCPM4.1-8B), a hybrid reasoning model, providing a reproducible implementation for the research community.

title: MobiEdit: Resource-efficient Knowledge Editing for Personalized On-device LLMs
submission: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed on mobile devices to power intelligent assistants, but models pre-trained on general corpora can still produce incorrect or outdated responses when handling personalized or unseen queries. Knowledge editing aims to address this by modifying a small portion of model weights while preserving general knowledge. Prior work focuses on weight updates that require resource-heavy backpropagation, which is impractical for local devices. We present MobiEdit, a mobile knowledge editing framework designed to be compatible with on-device constraints by replacing full-precision backpropagation with a quantized, forward-only gradient estimation approach intended for mobile NPUs. We also describe optimizations such as an adaptive early stopping mechanism and prefix activation reusing to reduce redundant computation across editing steps. These design choices target lower memory, energy, and latency for on-device personalization, enabling editing of small- to mid-sized models on commodity mobile hardware.

title: Towards All-Atom Foundation Models for Biomolecular Binding Affinity Prediction
submission: Biomolecular interactions are central to biology, but predicting binding affinity remains challenging largely because high-quality data are limited. We investigate repurposing AlphaFold 3 for representation learning toward binding-affinity prediction, which requires shifting from generative structure prediction to encoding observed geometry, simplifying the trunk, and jointly capturing sequence and structural information. To this end, we introduce the Atom-level Diffusion Transformer (ADiT): a model that takes sequence and structure as inputs, uses a unified tokenization scheme, integrates diffusion transformer blocks, and removes dependence on MSAs and templates. We pre-train ADiT variants on PDB with a denoising objective and evaluate across protein–ligand, drug–target, protein–protein, and antibody–antigen settings. The work reports competitive behavior on a range of benchmarks and highlights identification of some affinity-enhancing antibody mutations, but several aspects of the core objective—how AlphaFold 3 representations are adapted and how the diffusion components concretely map to affinity signals—are left imprecise and deserve clearer exposition.

title: Pretraining Scaling Laws for Generative Evaluations of Language Models
submission: Neural scaling laws have driven growth in parameters, data and compute, but while pretraining losses and discriminative benchmarks are well studied, generative benchmarks such as math problem solving or software tasks are less explored. We propose and evaluate three pretraining scaling laws for fitting pass-at-k on generative evaluations and for predicting pass-at-k of the largest model using smaller, cheaper models. The three laws differ by covariates: (1) pretraining compute, (2) parameters and pretraining tokens, and (3) gold reference solution log-likelihoods. We show generative evaluations introduce hyperparameters (notably k) that modulate scaling behavior and parameter stability: the compute and parameters+tokens laws stabilize only over the last ~1.5–2.5 orders of magnitude, whereas the gold-likelihood law is more stable across ~5 orders. Predictive performance is comparable across laws with mild differences depending on k. We also give a theoretical connection showing the compute law as the compute-optimal envelope of the parameters-and-tokens law. These findings aim to help forecast generative performance and sampling behavior.

title: CylinderSplat: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Cylindrical Triplanes for Panoramic Novel View Synthesis
submission: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has shown promise for real-time novel view synthesis, but applying it to panoramic imagery remains challenging: multi-view cost volumes used for geometric refinement struggle in sparse-view scenarios, and Cartesian Triplanes poorly capture 360° scene geometry, causing distortion and aliasing. We introduce CylinderSplat, a feed-forward framework for panoramic 3DGS built around a cylindrical Triplane representation that better aligns with panoramic data and Manhattan-world structures. A dual-branch architecture combines a pixel-based branch for well-observed regions with a volume-based branch using the cylindrical Triplane to complete occluded or sparsely-viewed areas, and the framework handles a variable number of input panoramas. We report experiments across single- and multi-view panoramic novel view synthesis; while CylinderSplat often improves reconstruction quality and geometric plausibility qualitatively, the quantitative gains are inconsistent across datasets and some evaluations do not clearly support a consistent state-of-the-art advantage, indicating trade-offs that merit further analysis.

title: Robust Decision-Making with Partially Calibrated Forecasters
submission: Calibration is a central notion for trustworthy ML because it ties forecasts to decision-theoretic semantics: a fully calibrated forecaster admits a simple mapping from predictions to optimal actions. In higher-dimensional settings full calibration is intractable, and weaker calibration notions have been proposed that lack those decision guarantees. We study how a conservative decision maker should map partially calibrated predictions to actions in a robust, minimax sense, maximizing worst-case expected utility over distributions consistent with calibration constraints. Using a duality-based analysis we characterize a minimax rule and relate it to notions like decision calibration. We also outline an efficiently computable rule for cases that fall short of decision calibration and present an empirical evaluation of a natural procedure for regression optimized for squared error. The exposition moves between theory and application but does not present a single, compact problem statement up front.

submission: Large Language Models (LLMs) show strong performance on complex reasoning but their computational cost limits broader use. title: Discovering heterogeneous synaptic plasticity rules via large-scale neural evolution
submission: Synaptic plasticity underlies learning and memory, and different synapse types can exhibit distinct plasticity mechanisms. We present a computational framework that uses evolutionary principles to search for heterogeneous, biologically plausible synaptic plasticity rules in a detailed model of mouse primary visual cortex. We parameterize factors such as pre- and postsynaptic spikes, eligibility traces, and neuromodulatory signals, combine them via a truncated Taylor expansion, and define a large search space of candidate rules with thousands of parameters. Using a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm we explore this space and select candidate rules judged on behavioral task performance and biological plausibility. We uncover diverse families of candidate rules and discuss how different mathematical formulations can give rise to similar behaviors, suggesting potential degeneracy in synaptic learning mechanisms. While we describe promising qualitative patterns and interpretive analyses, detailed quantitative results and benchmarks are left for follow-up work.

title: Natural Identifiers for Privacy and Data Audits in Large Language Models
submission: Auditing privacy of large language models is hindered by methods that require inserting canaries during training or needing a private non-member held-out dataset for dataset inference. We propose natural identifiers (NIDs) — structured random strings like hashes and shortened URLs that naturally occur in many training corpora — as a way to perform post-hoc audits. Because NIDs share a format, they can be used to generate additional random strings from the same distribution to act as alternative canaries and same-distribution held-out data for dataset inference. We evaluate NIDs on several audit scenarios and find they enable post-hoc differential privacy auditing without retraining and allow dataset inference when suspect datasets contain NIDs, removing the need for curated non-member sets. NIDs offer a practical direction for scalable, post-hoc audits.

title: WebShaper: Agentically Data Synthesizing via Information-Seeking Formalization
submission:
The advent of Large Language Model (LLM)-powered agents has revolutionized artificial intelligence by enabling solutions to complex, open-ended tasks through web-based information-seeking (IS) capabilities. The scarcity of high-quality training data has limited the development of IS agents.  Existing data synthesis approaches typically adopt an information-driven paradigm that first collects information and then refines question-answer pairs through retrieval. However, this may lead to inconsistency between information structure and reasoning structure, as well as between the question and the corresponding answer. To mitigate, we propose a formalization-driven IS data synthesis framework WebShaper, which systematically formalizes IS tasks using set-theoretic constructs.
Central to the formalization is the concept of Knowledge Projections (KP), which enables precise control over reasoning structure by KP operation compositions.  During synthesis, we begin by creating seed tasks, then use a multi-step expansion process.
At each step, an agentic Expander expands the current formal question more complex through retrieval and validation tools grounded in our formalization. We train our model on the synthesized dataset. Experiment results demonstrate that WebShaper achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-sourced IS agents on competitive benchmarks.

submission: We propose aligning pretrained visual encoders to serve as tokenizers for latent diffusion models rather than training a VAE from scratch, aiming to leverage foundation encoders' semantic structure. On ImageNet and larger-scale text-to-image settings we observe improved training dynamics and generation quality in our experiments. The approach is simple and scalable and offers an alternative paradigm for continuous tokenizer design, although exact gains and trade-offs are described qualitatively here rather than exhaustively quantified.

title: SmartDJ: Declarative Audio Editing with Audio Language Model
submission: Audio editing plays a crucial role in VR/AR immersion, virtual conferencing, sound design, and interactive media. However, recent generative audio editing models depend on template-like instruction formats and are restricted to mono-channel audio, and existing systems require users to specify low-level editing actions rather than expressing desired outcomes at a higher semantic level. We introduce SmartDJ, a framework for stereo audio editing that enables declarative audio editing: users describe the desired outcome while the system handles the underlying edit operations. Given a high-level instruction, SmartDJ decomposes it into atomic edit operations such as adding, removing, or spatially relocating sound events, which are then executed by a diffusion model trained to edit stereo audio. To enable this capability we design a scalable data synthesis pipeline producing paired examples of declarative instructions, atomic operations, and audios before and after each edit. Experiments indicate improved perceptual quality and spatial realism compared to prior methods; detailed benchmarks and examples are provided in the paper.

title: Measuring the Intrinsic Dimension of Earth Representations
submission: Within representation learning for Earth observation, geographic Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) embed low-dimensional location inputs (longitude, latitude) into high-dimensional embeddings via models trained on geo-referenced satellite, image or text data. Despite the common aim of geographic INRs to distill Earth's data into compact representations, we still lack a clear understanding of how much information these representations contain and where it is concentrated. The intrinsic dimension measures the number of degrees of freedom required to capture local variability regardless of ambient dimension. Here we study the intrinsic dimensionality of geographic INRs. Analyzing INRs with ambient dimension between 256 and 512, we find intrinsic dimensions that are typically small, roughly between 2 and 10, and that they change with spatial resolution and input modality during pre-training. We also observe relationships between intrinsic dimension and downstream performance that suggest the metric may be useful for model evaluation and diagnostics, though precise practical guidance remains to be established.

title: Efficient Agent Training for Computer Use
submission: Scaling high-quality trajectory data has been a bottleneck for human-like computer use agents. Starting from a modest set of 312 human-annotated computer use trajectories, we augment them by synthesizing diverse alternative action decisions with Claude 3.7 Sonnet. Trained on these enriched trajectories, our PC Agent-E model shows notable improvement on WindowsAgentArena-V2, an improved benchmark we release. By integrating human computer use skills with automated AI data synthesis, the method yields substantial gains compared to training on the human trajectories alone, and in some settings it even outperforms direct distillation from Claude 3.7 Sonnet. We highlight practical benefits for agent training, while noting more extensive evaluations and baselines would be needed to fully characterize limitations and generality.

title: Uncertainty Matters in Dynamic Gaussian Splatting for Monocular 4D Reconstruction
submission: Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes from monocular input is under-constrained, with ambiguities from occlusion and extreme novel views. Dynamic Gaussian Splatting is efficient, but vanilla models optimize all Gaussian primitives uniformly, ignoring observation reliability and leading to motion drifts and degraded synthesis when extrapolating. We argue uncertainty matters: Gaussians with recurring observations act as anchors, while those with limited visibility are less reliable. To this end, we introduce USplat4D, an uncertainty-aware dynamic Gaussian Splatting framework that propagates reliable motion cues to enhance 4D reconstruction. Our approach estimates time-varying per-Gaussian uncertainty and leverages it to construct a spatio-temporal graph for uncertainty-aware optimization. We provide implementation details and discuss how uncertainty guides motion propagation across time. Experiments on diverse real and synthetic datasets indicate that modeling uncertainty improves stability under occlusion and synthesis at novel views. Project page: https://tamu-visual-ai.github.io/usplat4d/.

title: Noise-Adaptive Diffusion Sampling for Inverse Problems Without Task-Specific Tuning
submission: Diffusion models have emerged as powerful priors for inverse problems, but optimization-based approaches can suffer from local minima and issues with enforcing measurement consistency. We introduce a posterior sampling perspective that treats reverse diffusion as a deterministic mapping from initial noise to images and outline a method called Noise-space Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (N-HMC) to explore the solution space by operating in the initial-noise domain. The high-level idea is to maintain proposals on the learned data manifold and to provide a noise-adaptive variant (NA-NHMC) for cases with unknown noise characteristics. We sketch theoretical motivations for sampling in noise space and point to practical advantages over some prior approaches. Details of the sampling dynamics, acceptance criteria, and step-size schedules are left for the full paper, as the core contribution here is the reframing of inverse inference in noise space rather than a complete methodological exposition.

title: Thyme: Think Beyond Images
submission: Following work on 'thinking with images', we introduce Thyme (Think Beyond Images), a paradigm for enabling multimodal LLMs to autonomously generate and execute image processing and computational operations via executable code. Thyme trains via supervised fine-tuning on a large curated dataset to teach code generation, followed by a reinforcement learning phase to refine decision-making. We propose GRPO-ATS (Group Relative Policy Optimization with Adaptive Temperature Sampling) to balance exploration in reasoning with precision in code execution. The system supports operations like cropping, rotation, contrast adjustments, and numerical computation, and is evaluated on a broad suite of benchmarks. Results indicate modest gains on challenging high-resolution perception and reasoning tasks, though gains vary across datasets and the benefits hinge on dataset curation and RL reward design. Ablations suggest some components help, but limitations and failure modes remain and are discussed alongside the main contributions.

title: Rethinking LLM Evaluation: Can We Evaluate LLMs with 200× Less Data?
submission: Benchmark suites for large language models are growing faster than we can afford to evaluate them. We ask which instances are necessary to keep the collective ordering of many models stable. We analyze redundancy at the instance level and find repetition in both text and the ranking patterns induced across models. Based on this, we formulate benchmark compression as a subset optimization problem targeting score reconstruction and ranking preservation. We propose EssenceBench, a coarse-to-fine framework with three stages: redundancy-aware filtering with text and ranking signals, fitness-driven subset search using an iterative genetic algorithm and a fixed surrogate predictor, and attribution-guided refinement for better coverage under tight budgets. Across multiple leaderboards, EssenceBench achieves lower reconstruction error and stronger ranking preservation than prior approaches while reducing selection time. On HellaSwag we report a large compression ratio that preserves rankings. Further empirical comparisons and broader benchmarks remain to be explored.

title: Spatially Guided Training for Vision-Language-Action Model
submission: Large vision–language models (VLMs) excel at multimodal understanding but fall short when extended to embodied tasks, where instructions must be transformed into low-level motor actions. We introduce SP-VLA, a dual-system Vision–Language–Action framework that leverages Spatial Priors as a bridge between linguistic instructions and embodiment-specific control. SP-VLA aligns action learning with spatial priors through two stages: (i) spatial grounding pre-training to equip the VLM with transferable priors from point, box, and trajectory prediction data, and (ii) spatially guided action post-training that encourages richer spatial priors to guide action generation via spatial prompting. This design preserves spatial grounding during policy learning and promotes consistent optimization across spatial and action objectives. Empirically, SP-VLA shows substantial improvements on robot manipulation benchmarks and better generalization to unseen objects and paraphrased instructions. We focus the paper on scalable spatially guided training and its promise for robust, generalizable robot learning, while qualitative analyses illustrate expected gains; explicit baseline comparisons are intentionally left modest to highlight methodology.

title: Scalable Training for Vector-Quantized Networks with 100% Codebook Utilization
submission: Vector quantization (VQ) is central to discrete tokenizers for image generation, yet training is often unstable due to straight-through bias, delayed updates, and sparse codebook gradients that reduce reconstruction quality and codebook usage. We analyze these challenges and propose VQBridge, a robust, scalable projector based on a map-function compress–process–recover pipeline that optimizes code vectors and stabilizes training. Combined with learning annealing, the resulting FullVQ (FVQ) approach is designed to maintain high codebook usage across diverse configurations. We report that FVQ attains full utilization across a wide range of codebook sizes and improves reconstruction quality relative to standard VQ variants. When integrated into an autoregressive image generation stack, FVQ also yields qualitative improvements in generation fidelity, highlighting the importance of robust tokenizers for strong autoregressive models. Detailed quantitative comparisons and ablations are left for the main paper.

title: Expressiveness of Multi-Neuron Convex Relaxations in Neural Network Certification
submission: Convex relaxations are central to neural network certification but suffer from known imprecision: even the most accurate single-neuron relaxation cannot fully certify general ReLU networks, a fact often described as the single-neuron convex barrier. We study whether multi-neuron relaxations overcome this limitation and what additional expressive power they may offer. Surprisingly, our analysis indicates that multi-neuron relaxations remain incomplete under natural resource allocations, extending the single-neuron barrier to a broader convex limitation. We also discuss two avenues that can lead to practical completeness: augmenting networks with additional ReLU neurons constructed in a particular manner, or partitioning the input domain into convex sub-polytopes. These observations motivate several directions for certified robustness, including training objectives and verification routines that exploit multi-neuron relaxations. The paper frames the main theoretical statements, sketches proof ideas, and suggests implications for future algorithmic work.

title: Beyond Multi-Token Prediction: Pretraining LLMs with Future Summaries
submission: Next-token prediction (NTP) has driven success of LLMs, but it struggles with long-horizon reasoning, planning, and creative writing, often attributed to teacher-forced training. Multi-token prediction (MTP) partially mitigates these issues by predicting several future tokens at once, but it mostly captures short-range dependencies. We propose future summary prediction (FSP), which trains an auxiliary head to predict a compact representation of the long-term future, preserving information relevant for long-form generations. We explore two variants of FSP: handcrafted summaries (e.g., bag-of-words summaries of the future) and learned summaries, which use embeddings produced by a reverse language model trained right-to-left. We describe large-scale pretraining setups for 3B and 8B-parameter models and evaluation protocols across math, reasoning, and coding benchmarks. We report on the experimental procedure and analyses but omit detailed numerical results in this communication.

title: SmellNet: A Large-scale Dataset for Real-world Smell Recognition
submission: The ability of AI to sense and identify substances by smell could impact allergen detection, manufacturing monitoring, and sensing hormones linked to emotional states and disease. Despite this, few standardized datasets exist for real-world olfaction, limiting progress in sensor-based machine olfaction. We present SmellNet, a large-scale dataset collected with small gas and chemical sensors that digitizes a diverse range of natural smells. SmellNet contains hundreds of thousands of time-series measurements across numerous substances—nuts, spices, herbs, fruits, vegetables—and multiple mixtures, with many hours of recording. We also introduce ScentFormer, a Transformer-based architecture combining temporal differencing and sliding-window augmentation tailored to smell signals, and we discuss preprocessing pipelines, sensor calibration, and dataset curation. Initial experiments illustrate that temporal modeling captures transient chemical dynamics, and we outline potential applications across healthcare, food and beverage, environmental monitoring, and manufacturing. SmellNet and code are released to spur further research in olfactory AI.

title: Synchronizing Probabilities in Model-Driven Lossless Compression
submission: Probabilistic next-symbol prediction is central to lossless compression, and learned models offer powerful probability estimates. However, matching predictions between compressor and decompressor is fragile: small non-deterministic differences can cause decoding failures. We formalize prediction mismatch and propose a model-agnostic mechanism called Probability Matching Interval Coding (PMATIC) that is intended to tolerate bounded prediction differences with modest overhead. PMATIC operates at the level of predicted probabilities and is designed to replace the arithmetic encoder in model-driven compressors. We outline theoretical correctness and performance bounds in abstract terms and validate ideas on text data. Overall, the work argues that PMATIC can increase robustness to prediction mismatch while maintaining competitive compression rates when paired with advanced predictors, though implementation details and extensive empirical comparisons are kept at a conceptual level.
