title: Bridging Draft Policy Misalignment: Group Tree Optimization  for Speculative Decoding
submission:
Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by letting a lightweight draft model propose multiple tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Yet existing training objectives optimize only a single greedy draft path, while decoding follows a tree policy that re-ranks and verifies multiple branches. This draft policy misalignment limits achievable speedups.  	
We introduce **Group Tree Optimization** (GTO), which aligns training with the decoding-time tree policy through two components: (i) Draft Tree Reward, a sampling-free objective equal to the expected acceptance length of the draft tree under the target model, directly measuring  decoding performance; (ii) Group-based Draft Policy Training, a stable optimization scheme that contrasts trees from the current and a frozen reference draft model, forming debiased group-standardized advantages and applying a PPO-style surrogate along the longest accepted sequence for robust updates. We further prove that increasing our Draft Tree Reward provably improves acceptance length and speedup.  	
Across dialogue (MT-Bench), code (HumanEval), and math (GSM8K), and multiple LLMs (e.g., LLaMA-3.1-8B, LLaMA-3.3-70B, Vicuna-1.3-13B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B, Qwen3-8B), GTO increases acceptance length by \(7.4\%\) and yields an additional \(7.7\%\) speedup over prior state-of-the-art EAGLE-3. By bridging draft policy misalignment, GTO offers a practical, general solution for efficient LLM inference. Code and draft models are available at https://github.com/hsj576/GTO.

title: Out of the Shadows: Exploring a Latent Space for Neural Network Verification
submission: Neural networks are everywhere but can be sensitive to small input changes, so formal verification is important for safety-critical systems. Many verification algorithms use reachability analysis or abstract interpretation to enclose possible outputs, but often verification is inconclusive because enclosures are conservative. To address this, we propose a specification-driven input refinement procedure that iteratively encloses the preimage for unsafe outputs to reduce the input set to those leading to unsafe outputs. We do this by transferring output specifications to input space via a latent space that arises from propagating a projection-based set representation through the network. Projection-based representations like zonotopes are described as "shadows" of higher-dimensional latent sets and so enable constraint transfer. We present an efficient verification tool that uses iterative refinement and zonotopes, which can be implemented with matrix operations for GPU speedups, and report competitive performance relative to top-ranking tools. The exact verification problem considered and its motivating examples are not clearly framed.

title: pFedMMA: Personalized Federated Fine-Tuning with Multi-Modal Adapter for Vision-Language Models
submission: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP generalize well in zero- and few-shot regimes, but efficient adaptation to decentralized, heterogeneous data is challenging. While prompt tuning is a popular parameter-efficient approach in personalized federated learning, it often struggles with unseen classes or domains. We propose pFedMMA, a personalized federated fine-tuning framework that leverages multi-modal adapters for vision-language tasks. Each adapter contains modality-specific up- and down-projection layers and a globally shared projection that aligns cross-modal features. Our optimization allows clients to adapt locally while collaboratively training the shared projection, and only the shared projection is communicated to reduce bandwidth. In extensive experiments across eleven datasets covering domain- and label-shift scenarios, we report improved trade-offs between personalization and generalization using pFedMMA, illustrating the promise of multi-modal adapters in federated settings. Implementation details, ablation directions, and training schedules are provided to facilitate reproduction.

title: Is Graph Unlearning Ready for Practice? A Benchmark on Efficiency, Utility, and Forgetting
submission: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are being used increasingly in sensitive, user-centric applications where regulatory frameworks (e.g., GDPR) require the ability to remove user data on demand. This has spurred interest in graph unlearning — removing the influence of specific training data from a trained GNN without full retraining. Despite several recent techniques, the field lacks a principled benchmark to judge whether unlearning is a practical alternative to retraining, or how to choose among methods for different workloads. We present a systematic benchmark structured around three desiderata: efficiency (is unlearning faster than retraining?), utility (does the unlearned model preserve predictive performance and align with a retrained gold standard?), and forgetting (does the model truly eliminate removed data’s influence?). Through experiments across datasets and deletion scenarios we synthesize trade-offs and limitations, and provide guidelines on when unlearning can be viable, while noting that most techniques still struggle at large scale.

title: Many-for-Many: Unify the Training of Multiple Video and Image Generation and Manipulation Tasks
submission: Diffusion models perform well across many visual generation and manipulation tasks, yet most methods train models for a single task (for example, text-to-video) or finetune pretrained models for related tasks. Training a robust T2V foundation model requires large, high-quality annotations which are costly, and many models only handle a few tasks. We propose a unified many-for-many framework to leverage available training data from diverse visual generation and manipulation tasks to train a single model. A lightweight adapter is designed to unify different task conditions, and we employ joint image-video learning to train models from scratch. We incorporate depth maps as a condition to better capture 3D structure. Two model sizes are considered and each can perform multiple tasks. By unifying training data and task conditions, the approach aims to produce a versatile model that benefits various generation and manipulation tasks, and we plan to release code and models.

title: Gradient-Based Diversity Optimization with Differentiable Top-$k$ Objective
submission: Predicting relevance is central across platforms—social media, entertainment, and commerce—but optimizing only for relevance often amplifies biases and produces homogeneous outputs that reinforce filter bubbles. We introduce a pairwise top-k diversity objective with a differentiable smooth-ranking approximation to incorporate diversity directly into gradient-based learning. Framed as a joint optimization of relevance and diversity, we analyze gradient trade-offs and propose two strategies: direct optimization, which modifies the learning objective, and indirect optimization, which reweights training data. Both approaches apply to training from scratch or fine-tuning existing relevance-optimized models. Recommendation serves as our evaluation setting where scalability and diversity are critical; through experiments we show that the methods improve diversity with negligible accuracy loss. Fine-tuning with the objective is especially efficient, often requiring only a few gradient steps to encode diversity at scale.

title: Beyond Pairwise: Empowering LLM Alignment With (Ranked) Choice Modeling
submission: Preference optimization for LLM alignment usually relies on pairwise comparisons, but richer human feedback formats like multiway comparisons and ranked lists offer more information. We introduce Ranked Choice Preference Optimization (RCPO), a unified framework that connects preference optimization with ranked choice modeling using maximum likelihood objectives. RCPO supports both utility- and rank-based choice models and can be instantiated with models such as the Multinomial Logit and Mallows-RMJ. We apply RCPO to contemporary instruction-tuned LLMs and examine its behavior across in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings. The paper sketches implementation details and comparisons to standard pairwise approaches and discusses how RCPO can be extended to incorporate different choice-theoretic assumptions.

title: GUIDE: Gated Uncertainty-Informed Disentangled Experts for Long-tailed Recognition
submission: Long-Tailed Recognition (LTR) remains a significant challenge in deep learning. Due to space we defer detailed quantitative results and full ablations to the main text, but report that GUIDE consistently improves robustness of multi-expert training under standard evaluation protocols.

title: Latent-to-Data Cascaded Diffusion Models for Unconditional Time Series Generation
submission: Synthetic time series generation (TSG) supports privacy, augmentation, and anomaly detection. A major challenge is modeling multi-modal distributions: latent-space diffusion captures high-level representations but can lose local fidelity, while data-space diffusion preserves local details but struggles to learn high-level modes. We propose L2D-Diff, a dual-space diffusion framework for unconditional TSG. L2D-Diff first compresses sequences into a latent space to model representation distributions efficiently, then guides a data-space diffusion to refine local details so generated series better reflect the true distribution. We evaluate on single-modal and multi-modal datasets and include ablations that explore the necessity of each component. Results indicate improvements in fidelity and representation coherence; we emphasize qualitative trends and the conceptual advantage of the dual-space design, without extensive head-to-head comparisons to particular baselines.

title: SCRIBES: Web-Scale Script-Based Semi-Structured Data Extraction with Reinforcement Learning
submission: Semi-structured HTML content—tables, lists, infoboxes—contains much of the web’s factual data but is difficult to extract reliably at scale. Existing approaches either lack generalization or are resource-intensive due to per-page LLM inference. We introduce SCRIBES, a reinforcement learning framework that exploits layout similarity across pages on the same site to generate reusable extraction scripts. Rather than process each page individually, SCRIBES learns scripts applicable to groups of structurally similar pages and iteratively trains on synthetic annotations drawn from CommonCrawl. In experiments we observe improvements in script quality and downstream QA accuracy, though absolute gains vary by site and are modest in many cases; the practical impact across diverse web domains is therefore somewhat limited. SCRIBES points toward more scalable, resource-efficient web extraction, but broader validation is needed.

submission: We investigate how reinforcement learning (RL) training affects cross-lingual reasoning generalization in Large Language Models compared to supervised fine-tuning (SFT). While results suggest RL can improve cross-lingual reasoning, we highlight limitations and note that conclusions depend on dataset and tuning details, motivating further controlled studies.
